records.title: Establish treatment intent before choosing systemic therapy
records.subtitle: Advanced and metastatic colorectal cancer · Colorectal
records.body: Confirm metastatic disease radiologically and histologically before treatment. Initial staging usually uses contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax, abdomen and pelvis. Use liver MRI when colorectal liver metastases appear resectable or potentially resectable. Consider FDG-PET to define disease extent when metastases may be resectable. Discuss treatment intent and resectability in a colorectal multidisciplinary team. Initially unresectable disease can be reassessed after systemic treatment 1 . At metastatic diagnosis: Test mismatch-repair or microsatellite-instability status, KRAS and NRAS exons 2–4, and BRAF. RAS testing is mandatory before anti-EGFR treatment. In RAS wild-type disease, assess HER2 amplification by IHC or FISH when HER2 blockade may be relevant. Preserve adequate tumour tissue for these decisions 1 . The evidence-defined first-line branches depend on: Mismatch-repair or microsatellite-instability status. 2 BRAF V600E. 3 Extended RAS status and primary-tumour side. 4 Later-line options add these treatment-defining groups: HER2-positive, RAS wild-type disease. 5 KRAS G12C-mutant disease. 6 Cytotoxic chemotherapy is the comparator backbone for most proficient-mismatch-repair disease. Dual immunotherapy outperformed chemotherapy in first-line MSI-H/dMMR disease. 2 BRAF-directed treatment improved outcomes when added to mFOLFOX6 in BRAF V600E-mutant disease. 3

records.title: First-line treatment
records.subtitle: Advanced and metastatic colorectal cancer · Colorectal
records.body: MSI-H or dMMR disease Nivolumab plus ipilimumab is an evidence-supported first-line option for an immunotherapy-fit patient. At the prespecified interim analysis of the first of two dual primary endpoints, the first-line comparison randomised 303 patients on local MSI-H/dMMR testing. The primary efficacy analysis included 255 with central confirmation. 2 Nivolumab plus ipilimumab improved centrally reviewed PFS (24-month PFS 72% vs 14%; median not reached vs 5.9 months). Proportional hazards were violated, so no hazard ratio was reported. Prespecified 24-month restricted-mean PFS was 19.2 versus 8.6 months, a difference of 10.6 months (95% CI 8.4–12.9) without separate alpha allocation. Safety was a key exploratory, untested endpoint. In the all-treated population, grade 3–4 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 23% with dual immunotherapy and 48% with chemotherapy; two treatment-related deaths occurred with dual immunotherapy. Overall survival was not reported at this interim analysis. The second primary endpoint and all secondary endpoints were untested. The CheckMate 8HW regimen was nivolumab 240 mg plus ipilimumab 1 mg/kg every 3 weeks for four doses, followed by nivolumab 480 mg every 4 weeks for up to 2 years. The chemotherapy comparator was investigator-choice mFOLFOX6 or FOLFIRI with or without bevacizumab or cetuximab. 2 Pembrolizumab monotherapy is another evidence-supported first-line option. KEYNOTE-177 compared pembrolizumab for up to 35 three-weekly treatments with mFOLFOX6 or FOLFIRI, with or without bevacizumab or cetuximab, in 307 previously untreated patients. Pembrolizumab improved final PFS (16.5 vs 8.2 months; HR 0.60, 95% CI 0.45–0.80). The crossed curves and violation of proportional hazards reflect a clinically important early-progression group. Overall-survival superiority was not established amid substantial crossover (HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.53–1.03). Grade 3 or worse treatment-related events were 22% versus 66%. Dual immunotherapy also improves disease control over PD-1 monotherapy across treatment lines. The nivolumab-plus-ipilimumab comparison included 707 immunotherapy-naive patients. Its primary analysis included 582 with centrally confirmed MSI-H/dMMR disease. 8 Nivolumab plus ipilimumab improved PFS over nivolumab (median not reached vs 39.3 months; HR 0.62) and increased response (71% vs 58%). In all 707 patients randomised on local testing, median PFS was 54.1 versus 18.4 months (HR 0.64). Grade 3–4 treatment-related events occurred in 22% versus 14%. The first-line-only comparison and overall survival remained masked. Before the randomised CheckMate 8HW evidence, CheckMate 142 9 established later-line activity for nivolumab plus low-dose ipilimumab in previously treated MSI-H/dMMR disease. It was a nonrandomised cohort, so its durable responses supported access and development but did not quantify benefit against chemotherapy. The US FDA approved nivolumab plus ipilimumab for unresectable or metastatic MSI-H/dMMR colorectal cancer in patients aged 12 years or older in April 2025. Local reimbursement and licensing may differ 10 . The small COMMIT interim conference-abstract analysis included 82 patients in a two-arm first-line comparison. 11 mFOLFOX6, bevacizumab and atezolizumab prolonged PFS over atezolizumab alone (30.0 vs 4.3 months; HR 0.439, 95% CI 0.23–0.84) and increased response (80.6% vs 46%). This result supports the combination over single-agent PD-L1 blockade within the reported comparison. It does not replace direct phase 3 evidence for nivolumab plus ipilimumab or pembrolizumab. For a tumour carrying both MSI-H/dMMR and BRAF V600E, the trials do not provide a direct comparison between first-line immunotherapy and BRAF-directed treatment. BREAKWATER required patients with MSI-H/dMMR disease to be ineligible for checkpoint inhibition. 3 CheckMate 8HW enrolled MSI-H/dMMR disease without selecting by BRAF status. 2 BRAF V600E-mutant, proficient-mismatch-repair disease Use encorafenib, cetuximab and mFOLFOX6 in first line. BREAKWATER enrolled 637 previously untreated patients with BRAF V600E-mutant, RAS wild-type metastatic colorectal cancer. Patients with MSI-H/dMMR disease had to be ineligible for checkpoint inhibition. The triplet improved confirmed central-review response in the initial primary set (60.9% vs 40.0%), final PFS (12.8 vs 7.1 months; HR 0.53) and interim OS (30.3 vs 15.1 months; HR 0.49) over investigator-choice mFOLFOX6, FOLFOXIRI or CAPOX with or without bevacizumab. Grade 3–4 adverse events occurred in 81.5% versus 66.8%. In February 2026, the US FDA converted first-line encorafenib plus cetuximab with fluorouracil-based chemotherapy to traditional approval for BRAF V600E-mutant metastatic disease 12 . After one or two prior regimens, encorafenib plus cetuximab provides a chemotherapy-free option. BEACON CRC randomised 665 patients to encorafenib, binimetinib and cetuximab; encorafenib and cetuximab; or cetuximab with irinotecan or FOLFIRI. The protected primary OS and response comparisons tested the triplet against control. The doublet efficacy analyses were secondary. Median OS was 9.0 months with the triplet, 8.4 months with the doublet and 5.4 months with control; response was 26%, 20% and 2%. The respective grade 3 or worse adverse-event rates were 58%, 50% and 61%. RAS and BRAF wild-type disease: choose by primary-tumour side For a left-sided primary, use a fluoropyrimidine-oxaliplatin or fluoropyrimidine-irinotecan doublet with an anti-EGFR antibody when response depth and survival are the priorities. PARADIGM compared panitumumab with bevacizumab, each added to mFOLFOX6, in 823 patients with RAS wild-type disease. In the left-sided primary population, panitumumab improved OS (37.9 vs 34.3 months; HR 0.82) and response (80.2% vs 68.6%). PFS was similar (13.1 vs 11.9 months; HR 1.00). Crossing survival curves at about 28 months limit the proportional-hazards summary. In the overall full-analysis population, OS was 36.2 versus 31.3 months (HR 0.84). In the right-sided subgroup, panitumumab did not improve OS (20.2 vs 23.2 months), PFS (7.2 vs 9.4 months) or response (55% vs 63%) over bevacizumab. These subgroup estimates do not support first-line anti-EGFR treatment for a right-sided primary. 4 PARADIGM addressed sidedness directly. 4 The earlier anti-EGFR trials established the predictive role of RAS status but did not settle that question: CRYSTAL added cetuximab to FOLFIRI in 1,217 EGFR-expressing, biomarker-unselected patients. The enlarged KRAS-evaluable analysis was retrospective and exploratory. In KRAS wild-type disease, cetuximab plus FOLFIRI was associated with longer PFS (9.9 vs 8.4 months; HR 0.70), OS (23.5 vs 20.0 months; HR 0.80) and higher response (57.3% vs 39.7%). All subgroup and treatment-by-KRAS p values were nominal and unadjusted. BRAF V600E was prognostic without evidence of a treatment interaction. Grade 3–4 events increased to 79.3% from 61.0%. PRIME added panitumumab to FOLFOX4. In wild-type KRAS disease, centrally reviewed PFS improved (9.6 vs 8.0 months; HR 0.80) and response was 55% versus 48%. The interim OS comparison of 23.9 versus 19.7 months did not reach statistical significance (HR 0.83, 95% CI 0.67–1.02). In mutant KRAS disease, PFS was worse with panitumumab (7.3 vs 8.8 months; HR 1.29), supporting biomarker restriction. FIRE-3 compared cetuximab with bevacizumab, each with FOLFIRI. The primary response comparison was negative (62.0% vs 58.0%; p=.18), and PFS was similar. Exploratory OS favoured cetuximab (28.7 vs 25.0 months; HR 0.77). The extended-RAS analyses were retrospective and reported no interaction test. CALGB/SWOG 80405 found no statistically significant OS advantage for cetuximab over bevacizumab when either was added to investigator-selected mFOLFOX6 or FOLFIRI (30.0 vs 29.0 months; HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.77–1.01). This publication did not report a primary-tumour-sidedness analysis. In CALGB/SWOG 80405, PFS was also similar (10.5 vs 10.6 months; HR 0.95), and response was 59.6% versus 55.2%. 17 Do not intensify the chemotherapy backbone to FOLFOXIRI solely because panitumumab is being used. TRIPLETE randomised 435 patients with RAS and BRAF V600 wild-type disease to modified FOLFOXIRI plus panitumumab or mFOLFOX plus panitumumab. Response (73% vs 76%), PFS (12.7 vs 12.3 months; HR 0.88) and R0 resection (25% vs 29%) did not improve. Gastrointestinal toxicity increased. RAS-mutant or otherwise non-actionable proficient-mismatch-repair disease For a patient eligible for intensive treatment, a fluoropyrimidine doublet plus bevacizumab is the control backbone. FOLFOXIRI plus bevacizumab increases response and disease control but also increases neutropenia, diarrhoea and neuropathy. The pre-biologic triplet trials show why patient and regimen selection matter: In the initial analysis of the phase 3 Italian GONO trial 19 , FOLFOXIRI improved investigator-assessed response (66% vs 41%), PFS (9.8 vs 6.9 months) and OS (22.6 vs 16.7 months) over FOLFIRI in 244 patients with favourable prognostic characteristics. Grade 2–3 neuropathy and grade 3–4 neutropenia increased. The phase 3 HORG trial 20 used a different FOLFOXIRI schedule in 283 patients and did not significantly improve time to progression (8.4 vs 6.9 months) or OS (21.5 vs 19.5 months). Alopecia, diarrhoea and neuropathy increased. These results do not justify treating every fit patient with a triplet. Use intensification selectively when a higher response probability may change symptoms or resectability, and review toxicity risk explicitly 21 . TRIBE compared FOLFOXIRI plus bevacizumab with FOLFIRI plus bevacizumab in 508 previously untreated patients aged 18–75 years. ECOG 0 was required above age 70. Triplet treatment improved the alpha-protected primary PFS endpoint (12.1 vs 9.7 months; HR 0.75). The prespecified but unadjusted secondary response analysis also favoured triplet treatment (65% vs 53%). The mature secondary OS analysis favoured triplet treatment (29.8 vs 25.8 months; HR 0.80); both were nominal. In unadjusted secondary safety comparisons, grade 3–4 neutropenia (50.0% vs 20.5%), diarrhoea (18.8% vs 10.6%) and neuropathy (5.2% vs 0) increased. 22 TRIBE2 tested FOLFOXIRI plus bevacizumab followed by reintroduction after progression against mFOLFOX6 plus bevacizumab followed by FOLFIRI plus bevacizumab. The alpha-protected primary PFS2 endpoint improved (19.2 vs 16.4 months; HR 0.74). Prespecified but unadjusted secondary analyses also favoured intensification for OS (27.4 vs 22.5 months; HR 0.82), response (62% vs 50%) and R0 resection (17% vs 12%); their p values were nominal. Grade 3–4 adverse events were 68% versus 46%. Deaths within 6 months were numerically higher with intensification (22 vs 13). 23 The patient-level evidence is consistent. A meta-analysis pooled 1,697 patients from five randomised trials. 24 The pooled analysis found longer OS (28.9 vs 24.5 months; HR 0.81), PFS (12.2 vs 9.9 months; HR 0.74), higher response (65% vs 54%) and more R0 resections (16% vs 12%) with FOLFOXIRI plus bevacizumab. Grade 3–4 neutropenia increased from 22% to 46% and diarrhoea from 8% to 18%. No treatment interaction was detected by BRAF status or prior adjuvant treatment. 24 Cytotoxic backbones and sequencing FOLFOX and FOLFIRI can be sequenced in either order without a demonstrated overall-survival difference in the direct GERCOR comparison. 25 The components were established in a series of first-line trials: The de Gramont trial added oxaliplatin to LV5FU2 in 420 patients. FOLFOX4 improved investigator-assessed PFS (9.0 vs 6.2 months), blinded-review PFS (8.2 vs 6.0 months) and blinded-review ITT response (50.0% vs 21.9%). OS was 16.2 versus 14.7 months and did not reach statistical significance; neutropenia, diarrhoea and neurologic toxicity increased. 26 The Saltz trial established irinotecan activity when added to bolus fluorouracil and leucovorin. IFL improved PFS (7.0 vs 4.3 months), OS (14.8 vs 12.6 months) and confirmed response (39% vs 21%) over fluorouracil/leucovorin; grade 3–4 diarrhoea occurred in 22.7% and severe neutropenia in 53.8%. 27 Douillard added irinotecan to infusional fluorouracil/leucovorin and improved the primary response endpoint (34.8% vs 21.9%), time to progression (6.7 vs 4.4 months) and OS (17.4 vs 14.1 months). Diarrhoea and neutropenia increased and were schedule-dependent. N9741 compared FOLFOX, IFL and IROX in 795 untreated patients. FOLFOX improved time to progression (8.7 vs 6.9 months; HR 0.74), OS (19.5 vs 15.0 months; HR 0.66) and response (45% vs 31%) over IFL, with less gastrointestinal toxicity and febrile neutropenia but more paraesthesia. IROX did not improve the primary endpoint over IFL. The GERCOR trial directly compared FOLFIRI followed by FOLFOX6 with the reverse sequence in 226 patients. 25 The sole primary endpoint, second PFS from randomisation through progression after second-line therapy, did not differ (14.2 vs 10.9 months). Secondary OS also did not differ (21.5 vs 20.6 months); no multiplicity adjustment or secondary alpha allocation was reported. First-line response and PFS were similar. In a prespecified but unadjusted secondary analysis, externally reviewed PFS during second-line therapy was longer with FOLFOX6 after FOLFIRI than with FOLFIRI after FOLFOX6 (4.2 vs 2.5 months). The p value was nominal. The publication did not state the denominator or precise time origin for this comparison. Toxicity differed by the first-line backbone. CAPOX is an evidence-supported oral-fluoropyrimidine alternative to FOLFOX. NO16966 randomised 2,034 patients and met PFS non-inferiority in the regulator-requested eligible population (7.9 vs 8.5 months; HR 1.05, 97.5% CI 0.94–1.18; upper margin 1.23). 30 ITT results were concordant, and OS was similar (19.8 vs 19.6 months). The trial regimen used oxaliplatin 130 mg/m² on day 1 and capecitabine 1,000 mg/m² twice daily on days 1–14 every 3 weeks. The earlier randomised phase 2 TREE programme 31 compared modified FOLFOX, bolus FOL and CAPOX schedules, first without and then with bevacizumab. It helped establish feasible oxaliplatin backbones but was not a phase 3 equivalence test. For a present-day CAPOX-versus-FOLFOX conclusion, use NO16966 rather than TREE. Modified capecitabine-irinotecan has narrower evidence than CAPOX: AXEPT 32 randomised 650 patients in Japan, China and South Korea after first-line treatment. Modified XELIRI, with or without bevacizumab, was non-inferior to FOLFIRI with or without bevacizumab for OS (16.8 vs 15.4 months; HR 0.85, upper 95% CI 1.02; margin 1.30). Grade 3–4 neutropenia was lower with modified XELIRI (17% vs 43%), while grade 3–4 diarrhoea was higher (7% vs 3%). Serious adverse events occurred in 15% versus 20%. This supports modified XELIRI as a second-line alternative in the studied Asian population. It does not establish that all capecitabine-irinotecan schedules are interchangeable with FOLFIRI. Adding bevacizumab Bevacizumab gives a modest average benefit when added to first-line chemotherapy. AVF2107g added bevacizumab to IFL in 813 previously untreated patients. 33 Bevacizumab improved OS (20.3 vs 15.6 months; HR 0.66), PFS (10.6 vs 6.2 months; HR 0.54), response (44.8% vs 34.8%) and response duration. Grade 3–4 adverse events increased to 84.9% from 74.0%. The NO16966 factorial comparison pooled XELOX and FOLFOX4. 34 Bevacizumab improved the coprimary PFS endpoint (9.4 vs 8.0 months; HR 0.83, 97.5% CI 0.72–0.95). OS did not reach statistical significance (21.3 vs 19.9 months; HR 0.89, 97.5% CI 0.76–1.03), and response was similar. Treatment discontinuation before progression was common, particularly in the bevacizumab arms. For a bevacizumab-naive patient progressing after irinotecan and a fluoropyrimidine, E3200 35 established second-line bevacizumab plus FOLFOX4: The three-arm phase 3 trial randomised 829 patients to FOLFOX4 plus bevacizumab, FOLFOX4 alone or bevacizumab alone. Adding bevacizumab improved OS (12.9 vs 10.8 months; HR 0.75), PFS (7.3 vs 4.7 months) and response (22.7% vs 8.6%) over FOLFOX4 alone. The bevacizumab-alone arm closed early for inferior efficacy. E3200 therefore supports the combination, not bevacizumab monotherapy.

records.title: Treatment-limiting safety checks
records.subtitle: Advanced and metastatic colorectal cancer · Colorectal
records.body: What the chemotherapy components do Fluorouracil is converted to metabolites that inhibit thymidylate synthase and disrupt RNA and DNA. Leucovorin stabilises the fluorouracil metabolite–thymidylate-synthase complex; it is a biochemical modulator, not an additional cytotoxic drug 36 . Capecitabine and tegafur are oral fluoropyrimidine prodrugs. S-1 combines tegafur with gimeracil, which slows fluorouracil breakdown, and oteracil, which reduces gastrointestinal activation. It is not dose-interchangeable with capecitabine 37 . Oxaliplatin forms platinum-DNA crosslinks. This mechanism does not determine sequencing; efficacy, organ function and cumulative toxicity still matter 38 . Irinotecan and its active metabolite SN-38 inhibit topoisomerase I. This mechanism does not substitute for regimen-specific evidence or hepatic-safety assessment 39 . Fluoropyrimidines Test for DPD deficiency before intravenous fluorouracil, capecitabine or tegafur. Do not use these fluoropyrimidines in known complete DPD deficiency. For partial deficiency, consider a reduced starting dose and titrate cautiously. EMA recommends pretreatment phenotype or genotype assessment and avoidance in complete DPD deficiency 40 . The current US capecitabine label advises DPYD-variant testing unless treatment cannot wait, while warning that a negative test does not eliminate risk 41 . For capecitabine, reduce the dose by 25% when Cockcroft–Gault creatinine clearance is 30–50 mL/min. Below 30 mL/min, a dosage has not been established. If there is no alternative, the label permits only an individualised reduced starting dose with close clinical and biochemical monitoring 41 . S-1 is authorised in the European Union for metastatic colorectal cancer when another fluoropyrimidine cannot be continued because of hand-foot syndrome or cardiovascular toxicity. This is a specific substitution setting, not evidence that S-1, capecitabine and UFT are generally interchangeable 37 . UFT, an older oral tegafur–uracil formulation, is retained here as a historical backbone. Its availability, licensing and partner regimen vary by jurisdiction; do not infer a contemporary dose or indication from older trials 42 . Oxaliplatin and irinotecan Oxaliplatin can cause acute and delayed peripheral sensory neuropathy. Assess symptoms before each cycle and modify or stop treatment according to severity and persistence. Renal impairment increases unbound-platinum exposure. Follow the label's renal-dose precautions rather than applying a regimen-independent shortcut 38 . Irinotecan can cause early cholinergic diarrhoea and delayed diarrhoea that may be life-threatening, as well as severe myelosuppression. Consider atropine for early cholinergic symptoms unless contraindicated. Start loperamide promptly for late diarrhoea using the product-label instructions. Treat late diarrhoea promptly and replace fluid and electrolytes. Add antibiotics when ileus, fever or severe neutropenia occurs. Interrupt treatment and then reduce subsequent doses after severe diarrhoea. Use caution in hepatic impairment. The label cannot recommend a dose when bilirubin exceeds 2 mg/dL because this population was not adequately studied 39 . Anti-EGFR treatment Cetuximab and panitumumab bind EGFR and inhibit ligand-driven receptor signalling. Cetuximab's IgG1 Fc can also recruit immune effector functions, but “antibody-dependent cytotoxicity” alone is an incomplete clinical mechanism and does not determine regimen choice 43 . Panitumumab can cause severe dermatologic and soft-tissue toxicity, progressive hypomagnesaemia and infusion reactions. Check magnesium and calcium before treatment, periodically during treatment and for up to 8 weeks after the final dose. Replete electrolytes as needed. Reduce the infusion rate for a mild or moderate reaction and terminate it for a severe reaction. Withhold or discontinue for severe dermatologic toxicity according to the label 44 . Cetuximab is a chimeric IgG1 EGFR antibody; panitumumab is a fully human IgG2 EGFR antibody. Cetuximab requires antihistamine premedication and carries a prominent infusion-reaction risk. Both require skin and electrolyte monitoring 45 . Start rash prevention with the first anti-EGFR dose rather than waiting for a severe eruption. In the phase 2 STEPP study 46 , moisturiser, sunscreen, topical steroid and doxycycline reduced grade 2 or worse skin toxicity over 6 weeks from 62% to 29%. Ask about eye pain, visual change and photophobia. Withhold treatment and obtain urgent ophthalmic assessment for suspected keratitis or ulcerative keratitis; corneal perforation is a rare label-listed complication. Bevacizumab Withhold bevacizumab for at least 28 days before elective surgery and for at least 28 days after major surgery. Do not resume until adequate wound healing. Monitor blood pressure every 2–3 weeks. Withhold severe hypertension that is not medically controlled. Discontinue for hypertensive crisis or encephalopathy. Monitor urine protein serially. A dipstick result of at least 2+ requires a 24-hour collection. Withhold at 2 g or more per 24 hours and resume below 2 g. Nephrotic syndrome requires discontinuation 47 . Other VEGF-pathway agents and refractory oral drugs Bevacizumab binds VEGF-A. Aflibercept is a soluble decoy receptor for VEGF-A, VEGF-B and placental growth factor. Ramucirumab blocks VEGFR-2. Their bleeding, hypertension, proteinuria, thrombotic, gastrointestinal-perforation and wound-healing risks overlap, but use each product's own dose-modification rules 48 . Ramucirumab also requires thyroid monitoring and its own proteinuria algorithm; do not import bevacizumab's thresholds 49 . Regorafenib inhibits several kinases involved in angiogenesis, oncogenic signalling and the tumour microenvironment, including VEGFR, RAF, RET, KIT, PDGFR and FGFR. Check liver tests before and during treatment because severe and fatal hepatotoxicity can occur 50 . Also anticipate hand-foot skin reaction, hypertension, diarrhoea, fatigue, mucositis and dysphonia with regorafenib. Use the ReDOS schedule below when an escalation strategy is appropriate; it does not remove the need for early review. Trifluridine/tipiracil combines a nucleoside metabolic inhibitor with a thymidine-phosphorylase inhibitor that increases trifluridine exposure. Check full blood counts before and during each cycle because severe myelosuppression can occur 51 . Fruquintinib is an oral VEGFR inhibitor. Monitor for hypertension, proteinuria, hand-foot skin reaction, haemorrhage, arterial thrombosis, gastrointestinal perforation and wound-healing complications 52 .

records.title: Treatment after progression
records.subtitle: Advanced and metastatic colorectal cancer · Colorectal
records.body: Second-line treatment After progression on bevacizumab-containing first-line treatment, these approaches produced modest survival gains in the corresponding trial populations: Switch the cytotoxic backbone while continuing bevacizumab. 53 Switch to FOLFIRI plus aflibercept. 54 Switch to FOLFIRI plus ramucirumab. 55 Continuing VEGF-pathway inhibition after progression produces a modest survival benefit: TML enrolled 820 patients whose disease progressed within 3 months after first-line bevacizumab-containing treatment. 53 Continuing bevacizumab with a switched chemotherapy backbone improved OS (11.2 vs 9.8 months; HR 0.81) and PFS (5.7 vs 4.1 months; HR 0.68). Neutropenia, diarrhoea, thrombosis, bleeding and gastrointestinal perforation were numerically higher. VELOUR added aflibercept to FOLFIRI after one oxaliplatin-containing regimen. It improved OS (13.50 vs 12.06 months; HR 0.817), PFS (6.90 vs 4.67 months; HR 0.758) and response (19.8% vs 11.1%). Grade 3–4 events rose to 83.5% from 62.5%. RAISE added ramucirumab to FOLFIRI after progression on bevacizumab, oxaliplatin and a fluoropyrimidine. OS improved to 13.3 from 11.7 months (HR 0.844) and PFS to 5.7 from 4.5 months (HR 0.793). Grade 3 or worse events increased to 79% from 62%. Anti-EGFR treatment after first line For RAS wild-type disease not previously exposed to anti-EGFR treatment, cetuximab or panitumumab can be used alone or with an appropriate chemotherapy backbone. Historical trials enrolled by narrower biomarkers; apply current extended-RAS selection rather than reproducing their original eligibility rules. NCIC CO.17 56 randomised 572 heavily pretreated patients with EGFR-expressing tumours to cetuximab plus best supportive care or supportive care alone. Cetuximab improved OS (HR 0.77) and PFS (HR 0.68), with an 8% response rate. Subsequent analyses established that benefit was confined to KRAS wild-type disease. BOND 57 randomised 329 patients with irinotecan-refractory disease to cetuximab plus irinotecan or cetuximab alone. Combination treatment increased response (23% vs 11%) and time to progression (4.1 vs 1.5 months); OS was 8.6 versus 6.9 months. In a later-line panitumumab trial 58 , OS in the RAS wild-type subgroup was 10.0 versus 6.9 months with best supportive care (HR 0.70). This result does not support panitumumab for RAS-mutant disease. In Peeters and colleagues 59 , second-line panitumumab plus FOLFIRI improved PFS (5.9 vs 3.9 months) and response (35% vs 10%) in wild-type KRAS disease. OS was 14.5 versus 12.5 months and did not significantly differ. Anti-EGFR rechallenge Rechallenge is different from continuing anti-EGFR treatment through progression. Consider it only after prior clinical benefit, an intervening anti-EGFR-free period and plasma ctDNA that does not detect a recognised resistance alteration. A negative plasma test can be false-negative when tumour shedding is low. Resistant RAS and EGFR ectodomain clones decline after anti-EGFR withdrawal, with a combined estimated half-life of 4.3 months in a serial-ctDNA analysis 60 . This provides the biological rationale; it is not, by itself, proof that rechallenge improves survival. CRICKET 61 treated 28 selected patients with cetuximab plus irinotecan. Response was 21%; median PFS was 4.0 months when baseline ctDNA was RAS wild type versus 1.9 months when a RAS mutation was detected. The analysis was small and nonrandomised. CHRONOS 62 excluded 16 of 52 screened patients because ctDNA detected resistance alterations. Among 27 treated with panitumumab, response was 30% and disease control 63%. Its single-arm design supports molecular selection, not a comparative survival benefit. REMARRY and PURSUIT prospectively explored longitudinal ctDNA before rechallenge. Their two-timepoint patterns remain hypothesis-generating and do not validate a universal “test twice” rule 63 . HER2-positive disease Define HER2 positivity as IHC 3+ or IHC 2+ with amplification by in-situ hybridisation. In chemotherapy-refractory HER2-positive, RAS wild-type disease, tucatinib plus trastuzumab has documented single-arm activity. MOUNTAINEER treated 84 patients in its primary combination efficacy set. Confirmed central-review response was 38.1%, including three complete responses. Median response duration was 12.4 months, PFS 8.2 months and OS 24.1 months. The single-arm design does not establish a comparative effect. Other HER2-directed evidence defines important alternatives and limits: HERACLES 64 treated 27 heavily pretreated patients with trastuzumab plus lapatinib. Response was 30% and stable disease 44%; the small single-arm study established proof of concept, not a preferred sequence. DESTINY-CRC01 65 gave trastuzumab deruxtecan 6.4 mg/kg every 3 weeks. In 53 patients with IHC 3+ or IHC 2+/ISH-positive disease, response was 45.3%, PFS 6.9 months and OS 15.5 months. Drug-related interstitial lung disease or pneumonitis occurred in 9.3%. DESTINY-CRC02 66 supported the lower 5.4-mg/kg dose: response was 37.8% versus 27.5% with 6.4 mg/kg, and PFS was similar. Cross-dose comparisons were not powered as a superiority test. SWOG S1613 67 compared trastuzumab plus pertuzumab with cetuximab plus irinotecan in 54 patients. PFS (4.7 vs 3.7 months) and response (34.6% vs 28.0%) did not significantly differ; the study does not establish superiority. Tucatinib plus trastuzumab has US accelerated approval for chemotherapy-refractory RAS wild-type, HER2-positive disease 68 . Trastuzumab deruxtecan has tumour-agnostic US accelerated approval for unresectable or metastatic IHC 3+ solid tumours after prior systemic treatment when no satisfactory alternative exists 69 . For trastuzumab deruxtecan, investigate new cough, dyspnoea or fever promptly. Permanently discontinue for grade 2 or worse interstitial lung disease or pneumonitis 70 . KRAS G12C-mutant disease For KRAS G12C-mutant disease, sotorasib 960 mg plus panitumumab is an evidence-supported option after a metastatic-disease regimen containing fluoropyrimidine, oxaliplatin and irinotecan, unless intolerance made standard refractory therapy appropriate. CodeBreaK 300 randomised 160 previously treated patients. The three groups received sotorasib 960 mg plus panitumumab, sotorasib 240 mg plus panitumumab, or trifluridine/tipiracil or regorafenib. The 960-mg combination improved centrally reviewed PFS over standard care (5.6 vs 2.0 months; HR 0.48). The 240-mg comparison did not meet its prespecified criterion. Overall survival was immature. Acneiform dermatitis and hypomagnesaemia were prominent. The US FDA approved sotorasib plus panitumumab for this post-fluoropyrimidine, oxaliplatin and irinotecan setting in January 2025 71 . Adagrasib plus cetuximab is an FDA accelerated-approval alternative after fluoropyrimidine, oxaliplatin and irinotecan. In the pooled KRYSTAL-1 efficacy population of 94 patients, response was 34% and median response duration 5.8 months; 31% of responses lasted at least 6 months. The regimen is supported by nonrandomised activity, not a direct comparison with sotorasib plus panitumumab 72 . Maintenance after induction Maintenance reduces treatment burden after disease control; it is not a single universal regimen. Base the choice on the induction biologic, residual neuropathy, response, resectability, patient preference and whether a treatment-free interval is acceptable. After oxaliplatin-based induction without a biologic: OPTIMOX1 73 found similar PFS (9.0 vs 8.7 months) and OS (19.3 vs 21.2 months) for continuous FOLFOX4 versus six cycles of FOLFOX7 followed by fluorouracil/leucovorin and planned oxaliplatin reintroduction. Neuropathy was numerically lower with the stop-and-go strategy. OPTIMOX2 74 was a small, prematurely stopped comparison of fluorouracil/leucovorin maintenance with a complete chemotherapy-free interval. Maintenance prolonged disease-control duration (13.1 vs 9.2 months) and PFS (8.6 vs 6.6 months); the study was not powered to establish an OS effect. After fluoropyrimidine, oxaliplatin and bevacizumab induction: CAIRO3 75 randomised 558 patients to capecitabine plus bevacizumab or observation. Maintenance improved PFS2 (11.7 vs 8.5 months; HR 0.67), did not worsen global quality of life and caused grade 3 hand-foot syndrome in 23%. AIO 0207 76 compared fluoropyrimidine plus bevacizumab, bevacizumab alone and observation. Bevacizumab alone met its generous non-inferiority margin for time to strategy failure; observation did not. Rare protocol reinduction limits interpretation, and the authors preferred fluoropyrimidine plus bevacizumab. The randomised phase 3 Stop-and-Go study 77 supported capecitabine plus bevacizumab maintenance after six cycles of CAPOX plus bevacizumab rather than continuing oxaliplatin indefinitely. This specific schedule should not be generalised to all induction regimens. Bevacizumab alone has inconsistent value: SAKK 41/06 78 did not establish non-inferiority of treatment interruption to bevacizumab. Time to progression differed by 1.2 months, without a significant OS difference; the investigators judged bevacizumab-alone maintenance of little clinical value. PRODIGE 9 79 found no improvement in tumour-control duration, PFS or OS from bevacizumab during chemotherapy-free intervals after FOLFIRI plus bevacizumab. In MACRO 80 , bevacizumab alone after CAPOX plus bevacizumab did not formally establish PFS non-inferiority to continued combination treatment. Efficacy differences were not statistically significant, while cumulative capecitabine- and oxaliplatin-related toxicity fell. After anti-EGFR-containing induction: VALENTINO 81 found panitumumab alone inferior to fluorouracil/leucovorin plus panitumumab after FOLFOX plus panitumumab. Ten-month PFS was 49.0% versus 59.9%; grade 3 or worse toxicity was lower with panitumumab alone. PANAMA 82 found longer PFS with fluorouracil/leucovorin plus panitumumab than with fluorouracil/leucovorin alone (8.8 vs 5.7 months; HR 0.72). OS was not significantly different. ERMES 83 did not establish non-inferiority of cetuximab alone after eight FOLFIRI-cetuximab cycles to continued FOLFIRI plus cetuximab. Maintenance lowered severe toxicity but shortened PFS in the modified per-protocol analysis. IMPROVE 84 was a randomised, noncomparative phase 2 study of intermittent versus continuous FOLFIRI plus panitumumab. It does not prove non-inferiority. MACRO2 85 was also exploratory phase 2 evidence and cannot overturn the phase 3 ERMES result. Older or frail patients Do not use chronological age alone to define fitness. Use geriatric assessment to identify vulnerabilities outside routine oncology assessment and match intensity to function, organ reserve, cognition, social support, competing illness and treatment goal 86 . FOCUS2 87 enrolled 459 patients considered unfit for full-dose chemotherapy and began regimens at 80% dose. Oxaliplatin did not significantly improve PFS; capecitabine did not improve quality of life and caused more grade 3 or worse toxicity than fluorouracil. AVEX 88 enrolled 280 patients aged at least 70 years who were not candidates for a doublet. Capecitabine plus bevacizumab improved PFS (9.1 vs 5.1 months; HR 0.53) but increased grade 3 or worse treatment-related events (40% vs 22%). PANDA 89 was a randomised, noncomparative phase 2 trial in older patients with RAS/BRAF wild-type disease. Both FOLFOX-panitumumab and fluorouracil/leucovorin-panitumumab met their activity threshold; the less intensive regimen caused fewer grade 3 or worse chemotherapy adverse events. It was not an equivalence trial.

records.title: Refractory disease
records.subtitle: Advanced and metastatic colorectal cancer · Colorectal
records.body: Trifluridine/tipiracil plus bevacizumab RECOURSE established trifluridine/tipiracil over placebo after at least two standard regimens. Median OS improved to 7.1 from 5.3 months (HR 0.68). PFS was 2.0 versus 1.7 months, response 1.6% versus 0.4% and disease control 44% versus 16%. Grade 3 or worse neutropenia occurred in 38%, febrile neutropenia in 4%, and one treatment-related septic death occurred. TERRA 91 confirmed trifluridine/tipiracil activity in 406 Asian patients. OS was 7.8 versus 7.1 months, PFS 2.0 versus 1.8 months and disease control 44% versus 15%. The smaller absolute OS difference does not negate RECOURSE but shows population-level variation. SUNLIGHT tested bevacizumab plus trifluridine/tipiracil after no more than two prior advanced-disease regimens. OS improved to 10.8 from 7.5 months (HR 0.61) and PFS to 5.6 from 2.4 months (HR 0.44). Response remained low at 6.1%. Grade 3 or worse events occurred in 72.4% versus 69.5%, while serious events occurred in 24.8% versus 31.3%. No treatment-related deaths occurred. The trial regimen used trifluridine/tipiracil 35 mg/m² twice daily on days 1–5 and 8–12, with bevacizumab 5 mg/kg on days 1 and 15 of each 28-day cycle. The BiTS study 93 explored a simpler biweekly trifluridine/tipiracil–bevacizumab schedule in a small, single-arm phase 1b/2 cohort. Its PFS of 4.29 months and OS of 10.86 months are hypothesis-generating; do not substitute this schedule for SUNLIGHT solely on cross-trial comparison. Regorafenib CORRECT randomised 760 heavily pretreated patients to regorafenib 160 mg daily on days 1–21 of each 28-day cycle or placebo. Regorafenib improved OS (6.4 vs 5.0 months; HR 0.77) and PFS (1.9 vs 1.7 months; HR 0.49). Grade 3–4 treatment-related events occurred in 54% versus 14%. Hand-foot skin reaction, fatigue, diarrhoea and hypertension were prominent. One fatal liver injury was compatible with treatment causation. CONCUR confirmed activity in 204 Asian patients, some of whom had not received every available biologic. OS improved to 8.8 from 6.3 months (HR 0.55), PFS to 3.2 from 1.7 months and disease control to 51% from 7%. Dose interruption or reduction was required in 71%. Week-by-week regorafenib dose escalation is an alternative to starting at 160 mg daily. ReDOS compared weekly escalation from 80 mg to 120 mg and then 160 mg with starting at 160 mg. More evaluable patients completed two cycles and began cycle 3 with escalation (43% vs 26%). OS (9.8 vs 6.0 months; HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.47–1.10) and PFS (2.8 vs 2.0 months; HR 0.84, 0.57–1.24) did not reach statistical significance. Week-2 quality of life favoured escalation. Fruquintinib Fruquintinib is an oral VEGF-receptor tyrosine-kinase inhibitor. In FRESCO 97 , 416 patients in China received fruquintinib or placebo. OS was 9.3 versus 6.6 months (HR 0.65), PFS 3.71 versus 1.84 months, and response 4.7% versus 0%. Many had not received prior anti-VEGF or anti-EGFR therapy, limiting direct comparison with FRESCO-2. FRESCO-2 enrolled 691 patients after fluoropyrimidine, oxaliplatin, irinotecan, anti-VEGF treatment, biomarker-appropriate anti-EGFR treatment, and prior trifluridine/tipiracil or regorafenib. Fruquintinib improved OS (7.4 vs 4.8 months; HR 0.66) and PFS (3.7 vs 1.8 months; HR 0.32). Response was 2%. Grade 3 or worse events occurred in 63% versus 50%, notably hypertension, asthenia and hand-foot syndrome. The FRESCO-2 regimen was fruquintinib 5 mg daily on days 1–21 of each 28-day cycle. 98 Investigational later-line treatment STELLAR-303 99 randomised 901 patients with non-MSI-H/dMMR disease to zanzalintinib plus atezolizumab or regorafenib. In the planned intention-to-treat analysis, the primary OS endpoint was 10.9 versus 9.4 months (HR 0.80). PFS was a secondary endpoint (3.7 vs 2.0 months); formal superiority cannot be claimed under the prespecified hierarchy. At the final analysis announced on 22 June 2026, the other dual primary endpoint, OS in patients without active liver metastases, was negative: 15.9 versus 12.7 months (stratified HR 0.83, 95% CI 0.66–1.05; p=0.1185) 100 . In the all-treated safety populations, grade 3 or worse treatment-related events occurred in 268/446 (60%) versus 161/434 (37%); five versus one treatment-related deaths used the same denominators. The combination remains investigational. The US new-drug application is under review with a 3 December 2026 action date; regulatory review is not approval 101 .

records.title: Local treatment of metastatic disease
records.subtitle: Advanced and metastatic colorectal cancer · Colorectal
records.body: Oligometastatic disease is a distinct treatment situation in which all metastases may be eradicated. The ESMO framework generally uses one to five lesions, up to two metastatic sites, a controlled primary tumour and the ability to treat every metastatic site safely. This is a framework rather than an automatic indication. Disease size, number and location matter. Technical completeness and invasiveness matter. Performance status, frailty, comorbidity, life expectancy and patient preference matter. Discuss every potentially local-treatable case in a specialist multidisciplinary team and reassess during systemic treatment 1 . Do not debulk unresectable multiorgan disease routinely Do not add tumour debulking to chemotherapy for unresectable multiorgan disease solely to reduce macroscopic tumour burden. 102 ORCHESTRA enrolled adults with metastases in at least two organs and substantial tumour burden. Only patients with response or stable disease after induction CAPOX or FOLFOX with or without bevacizumab were randomised. Debulking at least 80% of metastases by surgery, radiotherapy or ablation did not improve OS (30.0 vs 27.5 months; adjusted HR 0.88) or PFS (10.5 vs 10.4 months; adjusted HR 0.83). Serious grade 2–5 events increased to 53% from 39%, including eight grade 5 events and four deaths attributed to local treatment. Intact asymptomatic primary with unresectable metastases Do not routinely resect an asymptomatic primary tumour when metastatic disease is unresectable; randomised evidence has not established a survival advantage 1 . JCOG1007/iPACS 103 stopped early for futility after randomising patients with an asymptomatic primary and unresectable metastases. Primary resection before chemotherapy did not improve OS (25.9 vs 26.7 months; HR 1.10). The pooled SYNCHRONOUS and CCRe-IV analysis 104 also found no OS benefit from primary resection before systemic treatment (16.7 vs 18.6 months). These trials do not apply when bleeding, obstruction or perforation requires local control. Liver-limited and oligometastatic disease For potentially curable liver metastases, offer either surgery alone or perioperative chemotherapy plus surgery. Choose and sequence these approaches in a multidisciplinary team with medical-oncology and hepatobiliary-surgery expertise. When perioperative chemotherapy is selected, ASCO recommends a total of 6 months across the preoperative and postoperative phases. Larger or more numerous metastases may favour perioperative treatment, but shared decision-making must include its harms 21 . Resectability is technical and biological, not a fixed lesion-count rule. The aim is complete removal while preserving adequate functional liver. Bilobar disease, vascular proximity, future-liver-remnant volume, extrahepatic disease, response trajectory and the feasibility of staged resection, portal-vein procedures or ablation all need specialist review 1 . The historical Fong cohort 105 reported 37% five-year and 22% ten-year survival after resection in 1,001 selected patients. Without an unresected randomised control, these outcomes show the possibility of long survival but do not measure the causal effect of surgery. Its clinical risk score used node-positive primary, disease-free interval under 12 months, more than one liver metastasis, largest metastasis over 5 cm and CEA over 200 ng/mL to estimate recurrence. It is prognostic, not an automatic rule for denying surgery. For synchronous resectable liver disease, primary-first, liver-first and simultaneous strategies are all used. Choose the sequence from primary-tumour symptoms, liver anatomy, operative risk and the need for systemic treatment; no single sequence is universally preferred 1 . Perioperative and postoperative trials do not show a consistent OS benefit: EORTC 40983/EPOC 106 randomised 364 patients with one to four resectable liver metastases to surgery alone or six FOLFOX4 cycles before and after surgery. Perioperative treatment improved PFS in eligible and resected analyses, but long-term OS did not significantly differ. JCOG0603 107 randomised 300 patients after liver resection to mFOLFOX6 or observation. Five-year DFS improved (49.8% vs 38.7%; HR 0.67), but five-year OS was 71.2% versus 83.1%; the trial does not establish an OS benefit. The phase 3 Ychou study 108 after complete liver-metastasis resection found no significant DFS improvement from adding irinotecan to fluorouracil/leucovorin. This argues against routine postoperative intensification with irinotecan. New EPOC 109 found harm from adding cetuximab to perioperative chemotherapy for resectable KRAS wild-type liver metastases. Median OS was 55.4 versus 81.0 months (HR 1.45); do not extrapolate anti-EGFR response activity in unresectable disease into this perioperative setting. Thermal ablation can be considered for small unresectable colorectal liver metastases or small liver oligometastases. After systemic therapy, stereotactic body radiotherapy is a weak, low-quality-evidence option for liver oligometastases in patients who are not candidates for resection 21 . CLOCC 110 was a small randomised phase 2 trial in 119 patients with fewer than ten unresectable liver metastases and no extrahepatic disease. Adding aggressive local treatment by radiofrequency ablation with or without resection to systemic treatment improved long-term OS (HR 0.58). It does not show that ablation is equivalent to resection. The older Berber series and similar nonrandomised ablation cohorts identified lesion size and number as prognostic. They are vulnerable to selection bias and should not be converted into universal cut-offs; use modern technical assessment and the randomised CLOCC boundary instead. For highly selected patients with permanently unresectable liver-only disease, transplantation is now supported by randomised evidence: TransMet 111 enrolled 94 patients aged 18–65 years with ECOG 0–1, resected BRAF-non-mutated primary disease and liver-only metastases controlled for at least 3 months after no more than three treatment lines. Liver transplantation plus chemotherapy improved intention-to-treat five-year OS to 56.6% from 12.6% (HR 0.37). This result depends on stringent selection, specialist transplant review and organ access; it is not a general alternative to chemotherapy. Conversion treatment for initially unresectable liver disease Define the technical reason for unresectability before treatment and choose a regimen whose response probability is proportionate to the chance of enabling complete local treatment. Reimage at short intervals and involve the liver team from the start; radiological disappearance does not guarantee eradication. For left-sided RAS/BRAF wild-type disease, an anti-EGFR doublet produces high response rates; PARADIGM, CRYSTAL and PRIME provide the disease-control evidence, while TRIPLETE shows no benefit from adding a third cytotoxic drug. For RAS-mutant or right-sided disease, use a bevacizumab-containing doublet or, in carefully selected fit patients, FOLFOXIRI plus bevacizumab. TRIBE, TRIBE2 and the patient-level meta-analysis quantify the benefit and toxicity. OLIVIA 112 was a small randomised phase 2 trial confined to initially unresectable liver metastases. FOLFOXIRI plus bevacizumab produced higher response and resection rates than mFOLFOX6 plus bevacizumab, supporting specialist consideration rather than a universal triplet rule. VOLFI 113 found higher response and secondary-resection rates when panitumumab was added to FOLFOXIRI in a randomised phase 2 RAS-wild-type population. The phase 3 TRIPLETE result is the stronger guide to current backbone choice and did not support triplet over doublet chemotherapy with panitumumab. Stop oxaliplatin when cumulative neuropathy compromises function. Avoid unnecessarily prolonged preoperative exposure because oxaliplatin is associated with sinusoidal liver injury and irinotecan with steatohepatitis; duration must be individualised rather than inferred from a response-rate table 114 . After conversion, decide between resection, ablation and combined approaches by the distribution of residual and pretreatment disease, future liver remnant and the ability to treat every original site. Peritoneal-limited disease Cytoreductive surgery plus systemic chemotherapy may be offered to carefully selected patients when complete macroscopic resection is feasible, there are no extraperitoneal metastases and treatment occurs in a specialised centre. Do not add oxaliplatin-based HIPEC routinely. ASCO concludes that harms outweigh benefits for this regimen 21 . The evidence separates the value of complete cytoreduction from the value of the intraperitoneal drug: The historical Dutch randomised study 115 compared cytoreduction plus mitomycin-C HIPEC and systemic treatment with older fluorouracil-based systemic treatment, with or without palliative surgery. OS was 22.3 versus 12.6 months. The outdated comparator and bundled intervention prevent attribution to HIPEC alone. PRODIGE 7 116 randomised patients only after complete or near-complete cytoreduction. Adding short-duration high-dose oxaliplatin HIPEC did not improve OS (41.7 vs 41.2 months; HR 1.00) and increased grade 3 or worse complications 31–60 days after surgery. Final phase 3 CAIRO6 117 results compared perioperative systemic treatment plus CRS-HIPEC with upfront CRS-HIPEC in 351 modified-intention-to-treat patients with resectable peritoneal-only disease. OS was 44 versus 39 months (HR 0.85; p=.28). Among 292 patients who underwent macroscopic complete or near-complete CRS-HIPEC, major 90-day morbidity was 49/138 (36%) versus 40/154 (26%). CAIRO6 does not support routine perioperative systemic treatment for every resectable peritoneal-metastasis patient. Its earlier conference subgroup suggestions are not a validated right-sided or synchronous-disease algorithm and should not override the final negative primary OS result.

records.title: Read the pathology report as a molecular map
records.subtitle: Colorectal cancer: molecular pathology, genetics and prognostic determinants · Colorectal
records.body: Use the current CAP Colon and Rectum Resection protocol 1 and the ICCR colorectal dataset 2 for synoptic reporting. Record tumour site and size, perforation, histological type and grade, depth of invasion, treatment effect, lymphovascular and perineural invasion, tumour deposits, margins, lymph nodes, pTNM/ypTNM and relevant ancillary tests. Histology and grade Adenocarcinoma is the dominant epithelial malignancy, accounting for about 90% of colorectal carcinomas. Neuroendocrine neoplasms, lymphomas, mesenchymal tumours and hamartomatous lesions are much less common and require their own classifications 3 . Report a specific WHO type when present. Mucinous adenocarcinoma and signet-ring-cell carcinoma require more than 50% of the corresponding component; lesser components should still be described 4 . Signet-ring carcinoma is rare, diffusely infiltrative, favours peritoneal spread and has a poor prognosis. It is enriched for MSI and can occur in Lynch syndrome, but is not specific for either 5 . Medullary carcinoma is a solid, lymphocyte-rich subtype strongly associated with right-sided dMMR/BRAF-mutant disease. Despite high-grade cytology, strictly defined medullary carcinoma has a relatively favourable outcome compared with conventional carcinomas of similar stage and grade 6 . Use the modern two-tier grade for adenocarcinoma NOS and mucinous adenocarcinoma: low grade when gland formation is at least 50%, high grade when it is below 50%. The inherited four-tier thresholds—well differentiated above 95%, moderately differentiated 50%–95%, poorly differentiated below 50%, and undifferentiated with no glands—are descriptive history, not the preferred current WHO/ICCR reporting system. Immunohistochemistry CK20, CDX2 and SATB2 support colorectal differentiation, but no marker is perfectly sensitive or specific. A panel and the clinical context are safer than a single stain; SATB2 plus CDX2 performs particularly well 7 . Medullary carcinomas frequently lose CK20 and CDX2. SATB2 or CDH17 may be retained, while calretinin and occasionally CK7 can be expressed; this is a caveat against excluding colorectal origin from an unusual immunophenotype 8 . MMR immunohistochemistry assesses MLH1, PMS2, MSH2 and MSH6, with retained staining in non-neoplastic internal controls. Paired loss patterns localise the likely deficient complex and guide reflex testing and germline assessment; dMMR also identifies a treatment-relevant phenotype. Sidedness is a gradient, not two diseases Right-sided cancers are classically polypoid or fungating exophytic masses; they can become bulky before obstructing and may present with occult bleeding or iron-deficiency anaemia. Left-sided cancers are more often annular or encircling “apple-core”/“napkin-ring” lesions, causing altered bowel habit or obstruction. These are tendencies, not diagnostic rules 9 . Right-sided tumours are enriched for MSI-H/dMMR, CIMP-high, BRAF V600E, mucinous and medullary phenotypes. Left-sided tumours are more often chromosomally unstable and TP53-altered 10 . Molecular frequencies change continuously from caecum to rectum, so a binary right/left table should not be used as a surrogate for tumour testing 11 . In metastatic disease, a right-sided primary is generally associated with poorer outcome than a left-sided primary and modifies anti-EGFR treatment interpretation. The effect is treatment- and time-dependent; sidedness is prognostic context, not a molecular result 12 .

records.title: Integrate pathological prognostic determinants
records.subtitle: Colorectal cancer: molecular pathology, genetics and prognostic determinants · Colorectal
records.body: Record proximal, distal and radial/circumferential margins and, where used, residual-tumour status: R0, no residual tumour; R1, microscopic residual tumour; R2, macroscopic residual tumour. The radial margin is the surgically created non-peritonealised soft-tissue margin; in the lower rectum it surrounds the specimen. Tumour at or within 1 mm is reported as involved. In rectal cancer, involvement predicts local recurrence and poor survival; evidence in colon cancer is less extensive 13 . Record every examined and involved regional lymph node: nodal positivity and burden are major prognostic determinants. Examine at least 12 nodes when possible; low yield weakens confidence in a node-negative stage. A tumour deposit is a discontinuous nodule in the lymph-drainage area without residual nodal, vascular or neural structure; deposits make a node-negative case pN1c, while their number is still reported when nodes are positive. After neoadjuvant treatment, prefix pathological stage with y and report tumour regression separately. Acellular mucin pools do not count as residual tumour for pT or positive-node assignment. Lymphovascular invasion, perineural invasion and an infiltrative rather than pushing border are adverse pathological features. Tumour budding is a single tumour cell or cluster of no more than four cells at the invasive front and is a morphological correlate of epithelial–mesenchymal transition. Count the hotspot in 0.785 mm² and report Bd1 (0–4), Bd2 (5–9) or Bd3 (at least 10) 14 . Assess budding only in non-mucinous, non-signet-ring-cell adenocarcinoma areas. Do not report it in colon or rectal adenocarcinomas resected after neoadjuvant therapy. When applicable, budding is distinct from grade and predicts nodal metastasis in pT1 and recurrence in stage II disease. For resected stage IIA (T3) colon cancer, the following pathological and presentation features contribute to recurrence-risk assessment. See Early colon cancer for adjuvant-treatment selection. 15 Fewer than 12 lymph nodes sampled. Perineural or lymphovascular invasion. Poorly or undifferentiated tumour grade, except that poor differentiation is not a high-risk prognostic factor in dMMR/MSI tumours. Intestinal obstruction or tumour perforation. Bd3 tumour budding, meaning at least 10 buds per 0.785 mm².

records.title: Establish mismatch-repair and microsatellite status
records.subtitle: Colorectal cancer: molecular pathology, genetics and prognostic determinants · Colorectal
records.body: MMR corrects base–base mismatches and small insertion/deletion loops. Functional loss of MLH1, PMS2, MSH2 or MSH6 produces dMMR and may create MSI-H; dMMR is a protein/function result, whereas MSI-H is a DNA phenotype. Test every colorectal cancer for MMR/MSI to screen for Lynch syndrome, inform prognosis and guide therapy 16 . IHC and molecular testing are complementary. IHC can localise protein loss; PCR compares microsatellite lengths, and validated NGS assays infer MSI across many loci. A discordant or technically inadequate result warrants review or repeat testing rather than forced classification. Do not apply one universal percentage threshold. The historical Bethesda five-marker panel called MSI-H when at least two of five markers were unstable; modern mononucleotide panels and NGS assays use validated, platform-specific cut-offs. MSI-low is assay-defined and is generally managed like MSS rather than as a weak form of MSI-H 17 . Approximately 15% of colorectal cancers are dMMR/MSI-H. Most sporadic cases result from somatic MLH1-promoter methylation, often with CIMP-high/BRAF V600E biology; a minority reflect Lynch syndrome, and some unexplained cases have double-somatic MMR alterations 18 . Typical morphology includes proximal location, mucinous or medullary differentiation, poor gland formation, tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes and a Crohn-like peritumoural lymphoid response. These features should prompt testing but cannot replace universal MMR/MSI assessment. In non-metastatic disease, dMMR/MSI-H—especially stage II—is generally associated with a favourable prognosis. BRAF V600E can modify prognosis, particularly in MSS disease, so neither marker should be interpreted without stage and the other marker 19 . dMMR/MSI-H has stage-specific treatment implications and predicts sensitivity to immune-checkpoint inhibition in advanced disease. See Early colon cancer for stage-II adjuvant decisions and Advanced and metastatic colorectal cancer for checkpoint-inhibitor selection and trial evidence.

records.title: Interpret RAS, BRAF and HER2 separately
records.subtitle: Colorectal cancer: molecular pathology, genetics and prognostic determinants · Colorectal
records.body: Assess MMR/MSI, KRAS, NRAS and BRAF during the initial metastatic work-up, following current metastatic guidance 20 . Use validated molecular testing criteria and assess HER2 amplification in an appropriate advanced-disease context 21 . RAS RAS proteins are GDP/GTP molecular switches downstream of EGFR. Activating mutations impair GTP hydrolysis, lock signalling through RAF–MEK–ERK and make EGFR blockade ineffective. KRAS is altered in roughly 40% of colorectal cancers; NRAS is less common, while HRAS is not part of routine extended-RAS selection in CRC. Extended RAS testing covers KRAS and NRAS exons 2, 3 and 4: codons 12/13, 59/61 and 117/146. This corrects the older shorthand that considered only KRAS codons 12/13 or included HRAS. RAS mutation is a negative predictive biomarker for cetuximab or panitumumab; it is not simply a universal stage-independent prognostic marker. See Advanced and metastatic colorectal cancer for regimen-, line- and sidedness-specific anti-EGFR evidence. BRAF BRAF V600E accounts for most BRAF alterations and occurs in about 8%–10% of colorectal cancers. It is usually mutually exclusive with RAS mutation and enriched in right-sided, CIMP-high, sporadic MLH1-methylated disease. Cigarette smoking has been associated epidemiologically with MSI-H, CIMP-positive and BRAF-mutant CRC, but smoking is not a tumour biomarker 22 . BRAF V600E is a strong adverse prognostic factor, particularly in MSS and advanced disease. It is not an anti-EGFR exclusion biomarker equivalent to RAS: prediction depends on regimen and disease setting. See Advanced and metastatic colorectal cancer for BRAF-directed treatment and outcome evidence. In the post-hoc extended-RAS/BRAF analysis of 357 of 508 randomised patients with previously untreated unresectable metastatic colorectal cancer in TRIBE , median overall survival was 37.1 months in RAS/BRAF-wild-type disease, 25.6 months in RAS-mutant disease and 13.4 months in BRAF-mutant disease. The global likelihood-ratio p<0.0001 was nominal and unadjusted for multiplicity. HER2 ERBB2/HER2 amplification or overexpression occurs in approximately 2%–5% of colorectal cancers and is enriched in RAS/BRAF-wild-type disease. Use colorectal-specific IHC/ISH or validated NGS criteria; breast and gastric scoring should not be imported uncritically 24 . HER2 amplification can bypass EGFR and contribute to primary or acquired anti-EGFR resistance. That association is not absolute and should not replace RAS/BRAF testing. HER2 is also directly actionable in selected refractory metastatic disease. See Advanced and metastatic colorectal cancer for HER2-directed regimens and outcome evidence. c-MYC activation and VEGF-driven angiogenesis are central CRC biology, but neither is a routine standalone tumour-selection biomarker. Source-quality correction: legacy material lists DH1 , but no recognised colorectal biomarker by that name was identified in current CAP/ASCO/AMP or ESMO biomarker scopes. Do not interpret it as IDH1 or use it clinically.

records.title: Use consensus molecular subtype as a biological classification
records.subtitle: Colorectal cancer: molecular pathology, genetics and prognostic determinants · Colorectal
records.body: The consensus molecular subtype classifier 25 is transcriptomic taxonomy, not a replacement for validated clinical biomarkers. Mixed or unclassifiable samples occur, and routine treatment selection by CMS is not established. CMS1, MSI immune (14%): hypermutated, MSI-rich, CIMP-high, BRAF-enriched and strongly immune-activated; often right-sided and female. It can have favourable outcome before relapse but poor survival after relapse. CMS2, canonical (37%): epithelial, with WNT and MYC activation; more often left-sided and generally the most favourable CMS outcome. CMS3, metabolic (13%): epithelial, metabolically dysregulated and KRAS-enriched; outcome is intermediate. CMS4, mesenchymal (23%): TGF-β activation, stromal invasion and angiogenesis; more advanced presentation and the worst relapse-free and overall survival. Approximately 13% have mixed features, reflecting technical admixture, transition states or intratumour heterogeneity.

records.title: Recognise hereditary colorectal cancer syndromes
records.subtitle: Colorectal cancer: molecular pathology, genetics and prognostic determinants · Colorectal
records.body: Use phenotype, tumour testing, pedigree and germline testing together; manage each syndrome according to current hereditary gastrointestinal cancer guidance 26 . A negative single-gene result does not turn a strongly suggestive family history into average risk. Lynch syndrome: autosomal-dominant pathogenic variants in MLH1, MSH2, MSH6 or PMS2, or EPCAM deletions that silence MSH2. A dMMR/MSI-H tumour is a screening signal, not a Lynch diagnosis; sporadic MLH1 methylation and double-somatic MMR alterations are common alternatives 27 . Adenomatous polyposis: APC-associated familial adenomatous polyposis, including attenuated FAP, and autosomal-recessive MUTYH-associated polyposis. Other multigene-panel causes include POLE/POLD1 proofreading-associated polyposis and biallelic NTHL1. Hamartomatous polyposis: STK11-associated Peutz–Jeghers syndrome, SMAD4/BMPR1A-associated juvenile polyposis and PTEN-hamartoma tumour syndrome. Their extracolonic cancer spectra and surveillance differ. Familial colorectal cancer type X is the historical designation for Amsterdam-I families whose tumours are MMR-proficient, not merely families with no germline MMR variant. It has lower CRC and extracolonic-cancer incidence than Lynch syndrome and remains genetically heterogeneous 28 . “Lynch-like syndrome” is different: the tumour is dMMR/MSI-H but no germline cause or MLH1 methylation is found. Many such tumours have two somatic MMR hits; unresolved cases require genetics-led family-risk assessment.

records.title: Build the molecular pathogenesis model
records.subtitle: Colorectal cancer: molecular pathology, genetics and prognostic determinants · Colorectal
records.body: The classic adenoma–carcinoma model describes stepwise clonal selection: APC/WNT disruption is often early, KRAS activation can promote adenoma growth, and 18q/TGF-β-pathway and TP53 alterations are often later. It is a teaching framework, not an obligatory linear sequence; tumours can acquire different events in different orders 29 . Mismatch-repair route MLH1, PMS2, MSH2 and MSH6 operate as paired MMR complexes. Germline loss causes Lynch syndrome after somatic inactivation of the remaining allele; sporadic MLH1-promoter methylation is the commonest acquired route. Failure to repair replication slippage produces a hypermutated MSI-H tumour. Serrated/CIMP route CpG islands are CG-rich regulatory regions. CIMP describes concordant promoter hypermethylation across a defined marker panel, silencing tumour-suppressor or repair genes without changing DNA sequence. CIMP is biologically useful but assay panels and cut-offs are not fully standardised 30 . In the serrated pathway, BRAF V600E is closely linked to CIMP-high. When methylation silences MLH1, the tumour becomes dMMR/MSI-H; CIMP-high tumours without MLH1 silencing remain MSS. KRAS and BRAF mutations are usually mutually exclusive, but BRAF is not confined to MSI-H disease 31 . Chromosomal-instability and APC/WNT route Most non-hypermutated CRCs show chromosomal instability: aneuploidy, arm-level gains and losses, deletions and loss of heterozygosity. This route combines oncogene activation with loss of tumour-suppressor and apoptotic restraints; it can be sporadic or arise on a germline APC background. APC is the gatekeeper in the canonical adenoma route. In TCGA, APC was mutated in 81% of non-hypermutated CRCs and was commonly biallelically inactivated. One germline pathogenic variant causes APC-associated FAP, followed by somatic loss of the remaining allele. APC normally helps the destruction complex phosphorylate and degrade β-catenin. APC loss allows nuclear β-catenin/TCF transcription, sustaining crypt-cell proliferation, blocking normal differentiation and reducing apoptosis. WNT-pathway alterations occur in more than 90% of CRCs 10 . Other recurrent abnormalities TP53 on 17p encodes a stress-responsive transcription factor that can induce cell-cycle arrest, DNA repair, senescence or apoptosis. TP53 loss is common in non-hypermutated CRC and often accompanies the late transition to invasive carcinoma. Chromosome 18q loss can encompass SMAD2, SMAD4 and DCC. SMAD2/4 transmit growth-inhibitory TGF-β signals, while advanced cancers may co-opt TGF-β for stromal invasion and immune exclusion. These alterations are biologically important but 18q loss, DCC and TGF-β are not routine standalone treatment-selection tests. BRCA1/2 variants and broader homologous-recombination alterations occur in a minority of CRCs, but BRCA is not a canonical CRC pathway marker and does not currently establish platinum or PARP-inhibitor benefit. A pathogenic BRCA1/2 variant found on tumour-only sequencing may warrant germline follow-up; therapeutic action should remain trial- or indication-specific 32 . Biallelic germline MUTYH variants cause autosomal-recessive MUTYH-associated polyposis by disabling base-excision repair of oxidative DNA damage. The resulting tumours are enriched for G:C→T:A transversions and SBS18/SBS36 signatures; CRC may occur even without florid polyposis 33 .
