records.title: Stage and establish resectability
records.subtitle: Early colon cancer · Colorectal
records.body: Stage I–III colon cancer is treated with complete surgical resection when feasible. An oncological colectomy follows the tumour-bearing segment and its lymphovascular drainage: aim for 5–7 cm proximal and distal bowel margins, divide the mesentery at the origin of the named feeding vessels, and examine at least 12 lymph nodes (ASCRS 2022 colon guideline). Stage I disease is usually cured by surgery alone and does not require adjuvant chemotherapy. In a contemporary single-centre cohort of 1,467 radically resected stage I colon cancers, 5-year DFS was 98.3% and recurrence occurred in 1.76%; this is prognostic context, not a universal guarantee 1 . Postoperative management in stage II–III disease depends on pathological stage, recurrence risk, mismatch-repair status, fitness and the expected absolute benefit from treatment.

records.title: Plan postoperative therapy
records.subtitle: Early colon cancer · Colorectal
records.body: Adjuvant therapy treats occult micrometastatic disease after curative-intent surgery. A proportion of treated patients were already cured by surgery, so the expected reduction in recurrence must be balanced against short- and long-term toxicity. Recurrence may be locoregional, distant or a metachronous colorectal primary. In the historical ACCENT trial pool, 5,722/17,381 patients with stage II–III disease recurred; the risk depends strongly on stage and era, so this 32.9% pooled figure should not be applied to an individual patient 2 . Recurrence is concentrated early. Across 20,898 trial participants, adjuvant fluoropyrimidine chiefly reduced recurrence in the first 2 years, with some benefit through years 3–4; recurrence rates fell below 1.5% per year after year 5 and 0.5% after year 8 3 . Across 20,898 patients in 18 randomised colon-cancer trials, 3-year DFS was validated as a surrogate for 5-year OS 4 . A meta-analysis of observational cohorts associated each 4-week delay in starting adjuvant chemotherapy with worse OS and DFS (HR 1.14 for each). This association does not establish a causal 4–6-week or 8-week deadline 5 . Choose a stage III regimen The fluoropyrimidine options are oral capecitabine or infusional 5-FU/leucovorin. X-ACT randomised 1,987 patients with resected stage III disease: Regimen: capecitabine for 24 weeks or bolus 5-FU/leucovorin. Efficacy: capecitabine met DFS non-inferiority (HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.77–1.01) and OS non-inferiority (HR 0.86, 0.74–1.01). Superiority for relapse-free survival was not reached (HR 0.89, 0.78–1.02; nominal P=.104). Safety: the predefined grade 3/4 fluoropyrimidine toxicities occurred later and less often with capecitabine (P<.001). Review proton-pump-inhibitor need when prescribing capecitabine, but do not present the interaction as established pharmacokinetics. A retrospective stage II–III cohort associated PPI exposure with worse 3-year recurrence-free survival during CAPOX (69.5% vs 82.6%; HR 2.03, 95% CI 1.06–3.88) but not FOLFOX; prospective confirmation is lacking 7 . Oxaliplatin should be added for a fit patient with stage III disease: MOSAIC randomised 2,246 patients with stage II–III colon cancer to 6 months of FOLFOX4 or LV5FU2. Primary result: FOLFOX4 improved 3-year DFS to 78.2% from 72.9% (HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.65–0.91; P=.002). 2009 update: 5-year DFS was 73.3% versus 67.4% (HR 0.80, 0.68–0.93; P=.003). Stage III outcome: 6-year OS was 72.9% versus 68.7% (HR 0.80, 0.65–0.97; nominal P=.023), without a significant treatment-by-stage interaction. Ten-year update: stage III OS was 67.1% versus 59.0% (HR 0.80, 95% CI 0.65–0.99; nominal P=.016); stage II OS was 78.4% versus 79.5% (HR 1.00, 0.70–1.41; P=.980) 9 . NSABP C-07 randomised 2,492 patients with stage II–III disease to FLOX or bolus 5-FU/leucovorin. Primary result: in 2007, FLOX improved DFS (HR 0.80, 95% CI 0.69–0.93; P=.0034); 3-year DFS was 76.1% versus 71.8%. 2011 update: the DFS benefit persisted (HR 0.82, 0.72–0.93; nominal P=.002), while the prespecified secondary OS comparison did not reach nominal significance (HR 0.88, 0.75–1.02; P=.08). Safety: grade 3/4 diarrhoea occurred in 38% versus 32%, and enteropathy-attributed deaths numbered 5 versus 1. XELOXA randomised 1,886 patients with stage III disease to 24 weeks of CAPOX or bolus 5-FU/folinic acid. CAPOX improved DFS (HR 0.80, 95% CI 0.69–0.93; P=.0045); 3-year DFS was 70.9% versus 66.5%. At the final update, 7-year OS was 73% versus 67% (HR 0.83, 0.70–0.99; nominal P=.04), although no final-analysis alpha had been prespecified. 11 IMPACT provides the earlier fluoropyrimidine-alone foundation. In a pooled analysis of 1,526 patients with resected stage II–III disease, 6 months of fluorouracil/folinic acid improved 3-year OS to 83% from 78% (HR 0.78, 95% CI 0.62–0.97; P=.029) and event-free survival to 71% from 62% (HR 0.65, 0.54–0.78; nominal P<.0001). The historical comparison established postoperative systemic therapy in stage III disease. 1 year of levamisole plus 5-FU reduced recurrence by 41% (95% CI 23–54) and mortality by 33% (10–50) versus observation; levamisole alone had no detectable benefit. 13 In an unplanned age analysis, the treatment-by-age interaction was significant for OS (P=.0391) but not DFS (P=.0733); among patients aged 70 years or older, neither OS (HR 1.18, 95% CI 0.86–1.62) nor DFS (HR 1.03, 0.77–1.36) improved. Treat this as hypothesis-generating and individualise oxaliplatin by fitness, competing mortality, neuropathy risk and recurrence risk. 10 A later pooled analysis of 17,909 stage III participants included 4,340 aged 70 years or older. Time to recurrence was similar by age, whereas DFS and OS were shorter in older participants, showing the effect of competing mortality rather than proving loss of cancer control from oxaliplatin 14 . Select 3 or 6 months for stage III disease IDEA Collaboration pooled six randomised trials and 12,835 patients with stage III colon cancer. Primary analysis: three months did not meet non-inferiority to 6 months for DFS (HR 1.07, 95% CI 1.00–1.15; non-inferiority margin 1.12). Final update: non-inferiority remained unestablished for DFS (HR 1.08, 1.02–1.15) and OS (HR 1.02, 0.95–1.11). Design limit: regimen choice was not randomised, although the adjusted duration-by-regimen interaction in the primary report was P=.02. Use pathological risk and regimen together: T1–3 N1 disease treated with CAPOX: 3 months is a reasonable standard, with 6 months discussed when recurrence risk or uncertainty is greater. T4 and/or N2 disease: use 6 months of oxaliplatin-based therapy when tolerated. FOLFOX: 6 months provides the more secure disease-control estimate; the descriptive 3-month comparison did not meet non-inferiority. The regimen-specific estimates for 3 versus 6 months were: 15 FOLFOX: 3-year DFS 73.6% versus 76.0% (HR 1.16, 95% CI 1.06–1.26). CAPOX: DFS 75.9% versus 74.8% (HR 0.95, 0.85–1.06). Design limit: regimen was physician-selected rather than randomised, although the adjusted duration-by-regimen interaction was P=.02. The pooled risk analysis was expressly exploratory and post hoc: T4/N2 disease: 3-year DFS 62.7% versus 64.4% (HR 1.12, 1.03–1.23; nominal P=.01 for 6-month superiority). T1–3/N1 disease: DFS 83.1% versus 83.3% (HR 1.01, 0.90–1.12). Interaction: the duration-by-risk interaction was not significant (P=.11). N1c means tumour deposits without positive regional nodes; it was not an IDEA duration-stratification factor and should not automatically be relabelled N2. In an IDEA-France post-hoc analysis, pN1a/b and pN1c had similar DFS, but any tumour deposit was independently adverse: 3-year DFS 65.6% versus 74.7% and adjusted HR 1.36 (P=.0201) 16 . KCSG CO09-07 17 randomised 1,788 patients with high-risk stage II or stage III colorectal cancer. Three months of oxaliplatin plus six months of fluoropyrimidine met the overall three-year DFS non-inferiority criterion versus six months of both components (84.7% vs 83.7%; HR 0.953, 95% CI 0.769–1.180; non-inferiority P=.0065), with less neuropathy (58.3% vs 69.5%). The paper narrowly supports three months of oxaliplatin plus six months of capecitabine as an alternative in stage III disease. Non-inferiority was not established in the infusional-fluorouracil subgroup. Grade 2 or worse neurotoxicity in IDEA was approximately 14–17% after 3 months and 44–45% after 6 months. This difference is central when the absolute gain from longer treatment is small. Decide whether stage II disease needs chemotherapy Most patients with stage II colon cancer do not routinely require adjuvant chemotherapy. T4 disease carries sufficient recurrence risk that the guideline recommends offering treatment for stage IIB/IIC disease, while other high-risk stage IIA features support individualised discussion rather than an assumed uniform benefit. 18 The ASCO guideline recommends: 18 Do not routinely offer adjuvant chemotherapy for stage II disease overall. Offer it for stage IIB/IIC (T4) tumours. Consider it for stage IIA disease with fewer than 12 nodes examined, lymphovascular or perineural invasion, poor differentiation, obstruction, perforation or BD3 tumour budding. Do not routinely use fluoropyrimidine-only treatment for dMMR/MSI-H tumours. Do not routinely add oxaliplatin in stage II disease; discuss it when the recurrence risk justifies the toxicity. The principal adverse features are: pT4 disease. Bowel obstruction or tumour perforation. Fewer than 12 lymph nodes examined, with a risk of nodal understaging. Lymphovascular or perineural invasion. Poorly or undifferentiated histology, except where dMMR explains the morphology. High tumour budding, BD3 with at least 10 buds. In an unplanned exploratory stage II IDEA analysis, 5-year DFS was 87.3% with one risk factor and 74.8% with at least two; this is prognostic, and the duration-by-risk-factor-count interaction was not significant (P=.78). 19 Margin status and preoperative CEA need separate interpretation. A positive or indeterminate resection margin raises concern about residual disease and requires surgical/pathology review; elevated preoperative CEA is prognostic and supplies a postoperative baseline. Neither appears in the Baxter list as a stand-alone indication for stage II chemotherapy 20 . The stage II trial base is heterogeneous: QUASAR enrolled 3,239 patients with an uncertain indication for chemotherapy, mostly stage II. Fluorouracil/folinic acid reduced all-cause mortality (RR 0.82, 95% CI 0.70–0.95; P=.008) and recurrence (RR 0.78, 0.67–0.91; nominal P=.001) versus observation. The often quoted 3.6-point 5-year survival benefit in stage II disease was modelled from an assumed 20% baseline mortality rather than observed as an arm difference. Earlier evidence conflicted: the pooled IMPACT B2 analysis of 1,016 patients did not show significant event-free-survival or OS improvement with fluorouracil/folinic acid, whereas QUASAR later supported a small average benefit in an uncertain-indication population 22 . The exploratory stage II subgroup did not show a significant DFS or OS benefit from adding oxaliplatin; the treatment-by-stage interaction was not significant. 8 In the unplanned stage II subgroup, OS (HR 1.04, 95% CI 0.72–1.50; P=.84) and DFS (HR 0.94, 0.70–1.26; P=.67) did not improve; treatment-by-stage interactions were nonsignificant for OS (P=.38) and DFS (P=.37). 10 High-risk features are prognostic; they do not by themselves prove that oxaliplatin is predictive of benefit. A 2024 pooled analysis of 1,595 stage II participants from MOSAIC and C-07 found no OS benefit from adding oxaliplatin overall (HR 1.03, 95% CI 0.82–1.29) or within the current high-risk classification (HR 0.86, 0.63–1.18), and no tested factor or factor count predicted benefit 23 . When chemotherapy is selected: Fluoropyrimidine monotherapy is given for 6 months. If an oxaliplatin doublet is selected, either 3 or 6 months may be used after discussion of recurrence risk, expected benefit and neuropathy. 18 Regimen-specific IDEA estimates are descriptive because regimen choice was not randomised and the adjusted interaction was not significant. The stage II duration analysis pooled 3,273 patients with high-risk stage II colon or rectal cancer. Three months did not meet DFS non-inferiority to 6 months overall (5-year 80.7% vs 83.9%; HR 1.17, 80% CI 1.05–1.31; margin 1.20). Regimen was not randomised and the multiplicity-adjusted regimen interaction was not significant. Descriptive HRs were 1.02 for CAPOX and 1.41 for FOLFOX; grade 2 or worse neuropathy was 13% versus 36%. 19 ACHIEVE-2 randomised 514 patients with high-risk stage II disease to 3 or 6 months of mFOLFOX6 or CAPOX. Three-year DFS was 88.2% versus 87.9% (adjusted HR 1.12, 95% CI 0.67–1.87). The stand-alone trial did not define a non-inferiority margin or alpha, so it does not prove non-inferiority; grade 2 or worse neuropathy was 16% versus 43%. Avoid adjuvant targeted therapy outside a biomarker-defined indication VEGF and EGFR inhibition did not improve outcomes when added to standard adjuvant chemotherapy: NSABP C-08 : adding 1 year of bevacizumab to 6 months of mFOLFOX6 did not improve DFS (3-year 77.4% vs 75.5%; HR 0.89, 95% CI 0.76–1.04; P=.15). Grade 3 or worse hypertension, wound complications, pain and proteinuria increased. AVANT : the global DFS gate failed (P=.2024). Exploratory DFS HRs were 1.17 for bevacizumab-FOLFOX4 versus FOLFOX4 and 1.07 for bevacizumab-XELOX versus FOLFOX4. Five-year OS was 85%, 81% and 82%, respectively; grade 3–5 adverse events occurred in 73%, 76% and 65%. In N0147, cetuximab did not improve DFS in resected stage III KRAS wild-type disease (3-year 71.5% vs 74.6%; adjusted HR 1.21, 95% CI 0.98–1.49; nominal P=.08), and grade 3 or worse toxicity increased to 73.3% from 51.1%. 27 PETACC-8 : cetuximab did not improve DFS in KRAS exon 2 wild-type disease at the planned interim analysis (3-year 75.1% vs 78.0%; HR 1.05, 95% CI 0.85–1.29; P=.66), and increased rash, diarrhoea, mucositis and infusion reactions.

records.title: Use perioperative chemotherapy selectively
records.subtitle: Early colon cancer · Colorectal
records.body: Potential advantages of preoperative chemotherapy include earlier treatment of micrometastatic disease, tumour downsizing and better treatment completion. CT staging is imperfect, however, and exposes some patients with pathological T3N0 disease to chemotherapy that might have been omitted after upfront surgery. Neoadjuvant chemotherapy is not routine. When considered for radiologically high-risk, resectable M0 colon cancer, use multidisciplinary selection and explain CT overstaging and the absence of a confirmed universal DFS benefit: FOxTROT enrolled 1,053 patients with operable M0, CT-staged cT3–4 colon cancer and at least 5 mm of extramural extension, or at least 1 mm after the pilot. Disease control: six weeks of preoperative OxFU/OxCap reduced 2-year residual or recurrent disease to 16.9% from 21.5% (rate ratio 0.72, 95% CI 0.54–0.98; P=.037). Surgery: R0 resection was 94% versus 89%, and T4 disease at resection was 21% versus 31%. Staging limit: twenty-four per cent of control patients had pathological T3N0 tumours. OPTICAL 30 did not significantly improve 3-year DFS with neoadjuvant mFOLFOX6/CAPOX versus upfront surgery (82.1% vs 77.5%; HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.54–1.03). Pathological downstaging and a 7% complete response rate do not establish routine universal use. NeoCol enrolled 248 patients with CT-defined cT3 disease with at least 5 mm extramural invasion or cT4 disease. Three preoperative CAPOX cycles did not improve 3-year DFS over upfront surgery (83% vs 87%; P=.36). Only 38 of 56 planned events had occurred, so the result is nonconfirmatory. Fewer patients met postoperative criteria for chemotherapy (59% vs 73%; nominal P=.02). FOxTROT also contained a separate panitumumab substudy in RAS wild-type disease. It does not establish perioperative anti-EGFR therapy as standard.

records.title: Use ctDNA as a prognostic marker, not a routine escalation mandate
records.subtitle: Early colon cancer · Colorectal
records.body: Postoperative ctDNA identifies a group at high risk of recurrence, but a prognostic marker is not automatically a predictive treatment-selection test. In stage II disease, DYNAMIC randomised 455 patients to ctDNA-guided or clinicopathological management. Chemotherapy was given for ctDNA detected at week 4 or 7. Treatment use: the strategy reduced chemotherapy use to 15% from 28% (nominal RR for standard vs guided management 1.82, 95% CI 1.25–2.65). Efficacy: the strategy met 2-year RFS non-inferiority (93.5% vs 92.4%; difference 1.1 points, 95% CI −4.1 to 6.2; margin −8.5). Delivery: most ctDNA-positive patients received an oxaliplatin doublet, and the median time to chemotherapy was 83 days. Mature follow-up: at 59.7 months' median follow-up, 5-year RFS was 88% with ctDNA-guided management and 87% with standard management (difference 1.1 points, 95% CI −5.8 to 8.0); 5-year OS was 93.8% versus 93.3% (HR 1.05; P=.887) 33 . The strategy result does not erase prognosis: within the ctDNA-guided group, 3-year RFS was 86.4% for ctDNA-positive and 92.5% for ctDNA-negative disease. Clearance during treatment is also favourable, but these subgroup associations are exploratory and do not prove that changing therapy because of a ctDNA result improves survival. In stage III disease, DYNAMIC-III confirmed prognosis but did not validate treatment adaptation: 34 Prognosis: postoperative ctDNA-negative and ctDNA-positive patients had 3-year RFS of 87% and 49%, respectively (nominal P<.001). De-escalation: ctDNA-negative disease did not confirm non-inferiority (85.3% vs 88.1%; difference −2.8 points, 95% CI −8.0 to 2.3; margin −7.5). Escalation: ctDNA-positive disease did not meet the phase 2 superiority threshold (2-year RFS 51.1% vs 60.8%; HR 1.16, 0.87–1.53). GALAXY is prospective observational evidence. In the enlarged cohort, MRD-positive and MRD-negative patients had 24-month DFS of 20.57% and 85.10% (HR 11.99, 95% CI 10.02–14.35); the OS HR was 9.68 (6.33–14.82). Surveillance ctDNA positivity preceded radiological recurrence by a median 5.91 months. 35 Molecular intervention after completion of standard therapy has not yet improved outcomes. In ALTAIR, 243 ctDNA-positive, radiologically disease-free patients were randomised to trifluridine/tipiracil or placebo. DFS did not improve (median 9.30 vs 5.55 months; HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.60–1.05; P=.107), while grade 3 or worse adverse events increased to 73.0% from 3.3%. 36

records.title: Treat dMMR/MSI-H disease differently
records.subtitle: Early colon cancer · Colorectal
records.body: Determine MMR/MSI status before making stage II adjuvant decisions and before considering the dMMR-directed approaches below. This chapter owns the localized-treatment consequences of dMMR/MSI-H. Use the molecular chapter for assay interpretation, tumour biology, germline assessment and hereditary mechanisms rather than duplicating them here. Adjuvant chemotherapy Routine fluoropyrimidine-only adjuvant chemotherapy is not recommended for stage II dMMR/MSI-H colon cancer. 18 If shared decision-making leads to adjuvant treatment for stage II dMMR/MSI-H disease with T4 and/or another high-risk feature, excluding poor differentiation alone, use an oxaliplatin-containing regimen rather than fluoropyrimidine monotherapy; the supporting evidence is indirect. 18 The historical evidence explains this caution. In a pooled analysis of 1,027 patients, fluorouracil did not improve DFS in dMMR disease (HR 1.10, 95% CI 0.42–2.91); the stage II dMMR subgroup had worse OS with treatment (HR 2.95, 1.02–8.54), a small retrospective subgroup that should not be overread 37 . MMR has different prognostic and predictive questions. In the QUASAR correlative cohort, recurrence occurred in 25/218 dMMR tumours versus 438/1,695 pMMR tumours (RR 0.53, 95% CI 0.40–0.70), but fluoropyrimidine benefit in dMMR disease was imprecise (OR 0.81, 0.29–2.22) 38 . For oxaliplatin, MOSAIC suggested favourable dMMR subgroup effects for DFS (HR 0.48, 95% CI 0.20–1.12) and OS (HR 0.41, 0.16–1.07), but neither was conclusive. The C-07 tissue analysis found dMMR prognostic for lower recurrence yet no significant MMR-by-oxaliplatin interaction. These retrospective, underpowered subgroup findings support caution, not a stage III exclusion 39 . Adjuvant chemoimmunotherapy ATOMIC randomised 712 patients with resected stage III dMMR colon cancer: 40 Regimen: 6 months of mFOLFOX6 with atezolizumab followed by atezolizumab to complete 12 months, or mFOLFOX6 alone. DFS: at the second prespecified interim analysis, 3-year DFS improved to 86.3% from 76.2% (HR 0.50, 95% CI 0.35–0.73; P<.001). OS: the first interim analysis did not reach significance (5-year 89.7% vs 87.9%; HR 0.90, 0.55–1.47; P=.68). Safety: grade 3/4 adverse events occurred in 84.1% versus 71.9%. Neoadjuvant immunotherapy NICHE-2 treated previously untreated, resectable dMMR colon cancer: Regimen: nivolumab 3 mg/kg on days 1 and 15 plus ipilimumab 1 mg/kg on day 1, followed by surgery within 6 weeks. Surgery: timely surgery, a primary endpoint, occurred in 113 of 115 patients (98%; 97.5% CI 93–100); two myositis events caused delay. Response: among 111 eligible patients, pathological response was 98%, major pathological response 95% and complete response 68%. Maturity: no recurrence occurred at a median 26.2 months, but the 3-year DFS co-primary endpoint was immature. Other phase 2 strategies remain investigational: NICHE-3 42 gave two cycles of nivolumab plus relatlimab to 59 patients with locally advanced dMMR colon cancer. Pathological response was 97% and pCR 68%. IMHOTEP 43 evaluated perioperative pembrolizumab in localised resectable dMMR/MSI colorectal cancer. Among 72 efficacy-evaluable patients, pCR was 52.7%; grade 3 or worse immune toxicity was 15.7%, including one fatal event. Definition: major pathological response means 10% or less residual viable tumour.

records.title: Add evidence-based interventions after chemotherapy
records.subtitle: Early colon cancer · Colorectal
records.body: Structured exercise CHALLENGE randomised 889 patients with resected stage III or high-risk stage II colon cancer after completion of adjuvant chemotherapy. The comparison was a 3-year structured exercise programme versus health-education materials. DFS: structured exercise improved 5-year DFS to 80.3% from 73.9% (HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.55–0.94; P=.02). OS: the unadjusted secondary result also favoured exercise (8-year 90.3% vs 83.2%; HR 0.63, 0.43–0.94). Exposure: the intervention targeted at least 10 MET-hours per week above baseline within 6 months and maintenance for 3 years. The achieved between-group difference was 5.2–7.4 MET-hours per week during the programme; this does not support the legacy conversion of one MET to an hour of sitting. Safety: musculoskeletal adverse events occurred in 18.5% versus 11.5%. Aspirin Use aspirin only in an appropriate molecular context and after assessing bleeding risk. ALASCCA randomised 626 patients with stage II–III colon or stage I–III rectal cancer and a PI3K-pathway alteration to aspirin 160 mg daily or placebo for 3 years: Group A: in patients with PIK3CA exon 9 or 20 hotspot variants, aspirin reduced 3-year recurrence to 7.7% from 14.1% (HR 0.49, 95% CI 0.24–0.98; P=.04), the primary analysis. Group B: in patients with other PIK3CA, PIK3R1 or PTEN variants, the descriptive secondary result was 7.7% versus 16.8% (HR 0.42, 0.21–0.83); no multiplicity adjustment was performed. Safety: severe adverse events occurred in 16.8% versus 11.6%. ASCOLT 46 found no significant DFS improvement from aspirin 200 mg daily for 3 years after standard adjuvant therapy in its non-hereditary colorectal-cancer population. Do not extrapolate the PI3K-altered ALASCCA result to biomarker-unselected disease. In Lynch syndrome, CAPP2 47 compared aspirin 600 mg daily with placebo. In the intention-to-treat analysis, colorectal cancer occurred in 40/427 (9%) versus 58/434 (13%; HR 0.65, 95% CI 0.43–0.97; P=.035). Among 509 participants who took treatment for at least 2 years, the prespecified per-protocol HR was 0.56 (95% CI 0.34–0.91; P=.019). The effect became apparent only after about 4–5 years. CAPP2 does not establish the optimal current dose; discuss aspirin after gastrointestinal and bleeding-risk assessment and within hereditary-cancer guidance.

records.title: Surveillance after curative treatment
records.subtitle: Early colon cancer · Colorectal
records.body: Surveillance intensity should reflect stage, fitness for salvage treatment and local guidance. The following is the historical 2013 ASCO endorsement of a Cancer Care Ontario evidence-based schedule for resected stage II–III disease: History, examination and CEA every 3–6 months for 5 years. CT chest and abdomen annually for 3 years in most patients; include the pelvis when clinically indicated or when a rectal/high-rectal pathway applies. Clearing colonoscopy before surgery when feasible; if the colon was not completely examined, complete it after recovery. Colonoscopy at 1 year, then at 3 years and every 5 years if findings remain low risk; shorten the interval according to polyp findings. This dated schedule must be adapted if comorbidity, hereditary risk or prior endoscopic findings change the balance 48 . Current NICE NG151 specifies CEA plus CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis during the first 3 years but not a universal visit-by-visit cadence; follow the current local programme 49 . Recurrence risk falls substantially after 5 years, so routine cancer-directed imaging beyond that point needs a specific indication.

records.title: Define anatomy, risk and treatment intent
records.subtitle: Early rectal cancer · Colorectal
records.body: Select the treatment sequence by pelvic risk, resectability and the objective of organ preservation or radiotherapy omission. RAPIDO high-risk evidence applies to disease with at least one specified MRI feature: cT4, cN2, extramural vascular invasion, enlarged lateral nodes or mesorectal-fascia involvement. 1 PRODIGE 23 evidence applies to cT3 disease judged to warrant preoperative chemoradiation or cT4 M0 disease in patients with performance status 0–1 and age under 76 years. 2 STELLAR evidence applies to distal or middle cT3–cT4 or node-positive disease. 3 Radiotherapy omission: restrict response-directed omission to patients who meet the PROSPECT surgical and radiological criteria. 4 Organ preservation: offer watch-and-wait only after a clinical complete or near-complete response, with structured reassessment and access to prompt salvage surgery. 5 dMMR disease: ASCO recommends immunotherapy for MSI-H/dMMR locally advanced rectal cancer, but rates the evidence quality as low. Preserve the single-arm maturity, response-assessment, surveillance and salvage caveats below. 6 Complete staging before treatment Confirm histology and examine the whole colon when feasible; record the baseline CEA. Use CT of the chest and abdomen for distant staging. Use a dedicated high-resolution pelvic MRI for local staging. Report tumour height from the anal verge, sphincter relationship, pelvic nodes, mesorectal fascia, extramural vascular invasion and tumour deposits. Digital rectal examination adds fixation, height and sphincter information. Endorectal ultrasound can clarify selected early T1 versus T2 lesions when MRI is equivocal; it does not replace MRI for locally advanced disease. Test MSI/MMR before treatment. The 2024 ASCO locally advanced rectal guideline 7 makes MSI/MMR testing, dedicated pelvic MRI and structured synoptic reporting explicit prerequisites for treatment selection. This chapter owns the rectal-treatment consequence of MSI-H/dMMR. Use the molecular chapter for assay interpretation, tumour biology and hereditary assessment. Preserve function without compromising the resection plane Surgery follows TME principles for a resectable mid or low rectal cancer. Tumour height, sphincter or levator involvement, expected circumferential margin and baseline function determine whether a low anterior/coloanal resection is oncologically and functionally appropriate or an abdominoperineal resection is required 8 . Modern TME and multimodality treatment reduced pelvic recurrence into the 5–10% range in many series, but TME's independent survival contribution cannot be isolated from staging and perioperative treatment. Neoadjuvant therapy may facilitate sphincter preservation in selected low tumours; it does not guarantee a functional sphincter-saving operation. Use current practice anchors cT1–2 N0: after shared decision-making, options include transanal excision such as TAMIS/TEMS, endoscopic submucosal dissection or radical TME. Do not add preoperative radiotherapy outside a trial. cT1–2 node-positive or cT3–4: offer preoperative radiotherapy or chemoradiotherapy, then definitive surgery when the disease is resectable. Low rectal or MRI high-risk disease: favour TNT. Long-course chemoradiation with chemotherapy before or after is the stronger high-risk recommendation; short-course radiotherapy followed by chemotherapy is conditional. TNT systemic component: use 3–4 months of FOLFOX or CAPOX before or after chemoradiation, or after short-course radiotherapy. Three months of induction mFOLFIRINOX is an option for carefully selected fit patients. Selected middle/upper cT3 N0–N1 disease with clear radial margins and a planned sphincter-saving resection may use response-directed chemotherapy with selective chemoradiation, as tested in PROSPECT. When nonoperative management is a priority, favour chemoradiation followed by consolidation chemotherapy and require a concordant clinical complete response plus intensive salvage-capable surveillance. A current clinical complete response requires no palpable or visible residual tumour on digital examination and rectoscopy, and no observable residual tumour on MRI apart from fibrosis or treatment-related wall thickening, with no suspicious nodes. Discuss uncertainty, regrowth, salvage surgery and the surveillance burden before choosing nonoperative management. The current general radiotherapy schedules are long-course 50–50.4 Gy in 25–28 fractions with concurrent capecitabine or infusional 5-FU, or short-course 25 Gy in five fractions without concurrent chemotherapy. Selection is risk- and objective-dependent 9 . If long-course chemoradiation is followed directly by resection, a 6–11-week interval remains reasonable. The optimal interval after TNT with consolidation chemotherapy is not established; follow the selected regimen and restaging pathway rather than importing a single clock from older chemoradiation trials. These anchors reflect current NICE NG151 recommendations 10 , including no preoperative radiotherapy for cT1–2 N0 disease outside a trial and surgery after the selected neoadjuvant pathway for resectable cT1–2 N-positive or cT3–4 disease. After adequate R0 radical resection of pT1–2 N0 disease, routine adjuvant chemotherapy or pelvic radiotherapy is not indicated. Adequate local excision is definitive without routine adjuvant therapy only for carefully selected low-risk cT1 N0 disease; reported local recurrence is 7–21%, and adverse pathology or an involved/uncertain margin generally prompts radical resection. Pelvic recurrence is highly morbid and may require multivisceral salvage or pelvic exenteration. Refer potentially curable recurrence early to a specialist pelvic multidisciplinary team; historical local-failure percentages are not current counselling estimates.

records.title: Use postoperative chemotherapy selectively
records.subtitle: Early rectal cancer · Colorectal
records.body: Understand the historical postoperative evidence Older trials predated modern MRI, TME and TNT. They explain why postoperative pelvic treatment became standard but should not displace the current preoperative pathway. A 2001 individual-patient meta-analysis of 22 radiotherapy trials found the yearly local-recurrence risk 37% lower with postoperative radiotherapy than surgery alone; overall survival was only marginally different 11 . The 1985 GITSG four-arm trial found the lowest recurrence and longer DFS with postoperative chemoradiation versus observation, at the cost of greater toxicity; it did not establish an OS difference 12 . NSABP R-01 randomised 555 Dukes B/C cancers. MOF chemotherapy improved DFS and survival versus surgery, mainly in men; postoperative radiotherapy reduced locoregional recurrence from 25% to 16% but not DFS or OS 13 . A 2012 Cochrane review of older fluoropyrimidine trials estimated lower relapse (HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.68–0.83) and death (HR 0.83, 0.76–0.91) with postoperative chemotherapy, but could not resolve modern stage-specific use after neoadjuvant treatment 14 . Historical pooled analyses placed local failure below 10% for T1–2 N0, around 15–35% for T3 N0, and 45–65% for T3–4 node-positive disease. These are pre-modern risk estimates, not counselling figures for a patient treated with MRI selection, TME and contemporary neoadjuvant therapy 15 . Use a fluoropyrimidine if postoperative chemoradiation is required The 401-patient REKTUM-III phase 3 trial included postoperative and preoperative cohorts. Capecitabine-based chemoradiation met 5-year OS non-inferiority to fluorouracil (76% vs 67%; non-inferiority P=0.0004); 3-year DFS was 75% versus 67% (P=0.07). Hand-foot syndrome was more frequent with capecitabine and leucopenia with fluorouracil 16 . Historical postoperative sequence: two capecitabine cycles at 2,500 mg/m²/day on days 1–14 every 3 weeks, then 50.4 Gy with capecitabine 1,650 mg/m²/day on days 1–38, then three capecitabine cycles. The fluorouracil arm used two 5-day bolus cycles, then 50.4 Gy with continuous infusion at 225 mg/m²/day, then two further bolus cycles. Amended preoperative sequence: 50.4 Gy with capecitabine 1,650 mg/m²/day, surgery, then five 14-day cycles at 2,500 mg/m²/day. The fluorouracil arm used 1,000 mg/m²/day on days 1–5 and 29–33 with radiotherapy, surgery, then four 5-day bolus cycles at 500 mg/m²/day. These are the regimens tested, not the current preferred sequence. Do not routinely add oxaliplatin concurrently to postoperative capecitabine-radiotherapy. In a 589-patient Chinese phase 3 trial, 5-year DFS was 72.0% versus 71.1% (HR 1.07, 95% CI 0.79–1.44), with more grade 3/4 acute toxicity (38.6% vs 28.6%) 17 . Select FOLFOX after preoperative chemoradiation ADORE reported its long-term analysis in 2019 and tested postoperative oxaliplatin after fluoropyrimidine chemoradiation and total mesorectal excision (TME): 18 Population: 321 patients with ypStage II–III disease after fluoropyrimidine-only preoperative chemoradiation, R0 TME and performance status 0–1. Control: fluorouracil 380 mg/m² plus leucovorin 20 mg/m² on days 1–5 every 4 weeks for four cycles. Experimental regimen: FOLFOX every 2 weeks for eight cycles. Protected result: 3-year disease-free survival was 71.6% with FOLFOX and 62.9% with fluorouracil/leucovorin. Long-term result: in the post-hoc analysis, 6-year disease-free survival was 68.2% versus 56.8% (stratified HR 0.63, 95% CI 0.43–0.93; nominal P=0.018). Overall survival: 6-year overall survival was 78.1% versus 76.4% (HR 0.73, 95% CI 0.45–1.19; nominal P=0.21), without a confirmed benefit. Limit: signals in node-positive, stage III and pN2 disease were post-hoc subgroup findings and do not replace the primary analysis. Older subgroup: in 55 patients aged 65 years or older, the post-hoc disease-free-survival estimate was HR 0.60 (95% CI 0.21–1.67), with age-interaction P=0.90. The wide interval does not establish absence of benefit; the overall-survival subgroup was likewise inconclusive.

records.title: Prefer preoperative when pelvic chemoradiation is required
records.subtitle: Early rectal cancer · Colorectal
records.body: Establish the preoperative approach The German Rectal trial reported in 2004 and randomised preoperative against postoperative fluorouracil chemoradiation: 19 Population: 823 patients with ultrasound- and CT-staged, resectable cT3/cT4 or node-positive rectal cancer. Regimen: fluorouracil chemoradiation before or after TME; both groups received four postoperative cycles of single-agent fluorouracil. Local control: 5-year local recurrence was 6% after preoperative treatment and 13% after postoperative treatment. Pelvic relapse at 10 years was 7% versus 10% (P=0.048). Survival: 5-year disease-free survival was 68% versus 65% (nominal P=0.32), and 5-year overall survival was 76% versus 74% (primary-endpoint P=0.80). Protocol-radiotherapy toxicity: grade 3–4 acute toxicity was 27% versus 40%, and long-term toxicity 14% versus 24%. All-patient sensitivity analysis: acute toxicity was 25% versus 24%, and long-term toxicity 14% versus 15%. Late effect: anastomotic stricture was 4% versus 12% (P=0.003). Sphincter preservation: among 194 patients judged before randomisation to require abdominoperineal resection, 45/116 (39%) after preoperative treatment and 15/78 (19%) after postoperative treatment received sphincter-preserving surgery. Limit: the sphincter result was an actual-treatment-given subgroup without an interaction test. Local recurrence and sphincter preservation were secondary comparisons without multiplicity adjustment; the overall-survival primary endpoint was not met. Staging limit: clinical staging reflected the methods of its time, and 18% of the postoperative group had pathological stage I disease after resection. A smaller single-institution Korean phase 3 trial used capecitabine chemoradiation in 240 cT3, potentially resectable cT4 or node-positive cancers. Preoperative treatment did not improve local control or survival, but increased sphincter preservation among low tumours to 68% from 42% (P=.008); the low-tumour distribution was imbalanced 20 . Match short- or long-course treatment to the objective The historical Swedish and Dutch programmes established that preoperative short-course radiotherapy can reduce local recurrence versus surgery alone. The 2001 individual-patient overview estimated a 46% proportional reduction in yearly local recurrence with preoperative radiotherapy, while also showing increased early non-cancer mortality in older-era delivery; contemporary selection and technique matter. The Polish trial reported its long-term comparison in 2006: 21 Population: 316 patients with resectable cT3/cT4 rectal cancer, no sphincter involvement and a lower tumour margin accessible on digital examination. Regimen: 25 Gy in five fractions followed by TME within 7 days, or fluorouracil chemoradiation to 50.4 Gy followed by TME after 4–6 weeks. Response: complete response was 0.7% versus 16.1%, and involved circumferential margins 12.9% versus 4.4%, favouring long-course chemoradiation. Primary result: sphincter preservation was 61.2% versus 58.0%; the trial did not show an advantage for long-course treatment. Other outcomes: permanent stoma, local recurrence, disease-free survival and overall survival did not significantly differ. Toxicity: severe acute toxicity was 3.2% versus 18.2%. Limit: pathological response did not translate into better sphincter preservation or disease control. The Australasian comparison reported in 2012: 22 Population: 326 ultrasound/MRI-staged cT3 rectal cancers. Regimen: short-course radiotherapy, surgery and adjuvant chemotherapy, or long-course fluorouracil chemoradiation, surgery and adjuvant chemotherapy. Primary result: 3-year local recurrence was 7.5% versus 4.4% (P=0.24). Other outcomes: distant recurrence, 5-year overall survival (74% versus 70%) and late toxicity did not significantly differ. Response: pathological complete response was 1% versus 15%, favouring long-course treatment. Limit: this was a null superiority trial, not evidence of equivalence. Report treatment response with the current pathology scale The current CAP Modified Ryan tumour-regression score is: 0: complete response, with no viable cancer cells. 1: near-complete response, with single cells or rare small groups. 2: partial response, with residual cancer and evident regression. 3: poor or no response, with extensive residual cancer and no evident regression. The inherited 0–4 scale, in which 0 meant no regression and 4 meant complete response, is obsolete and directionally incompatible with the current protocol 23 . Do not routinely add concurrent oxaliplatin In one trial, pathological complete response was 16% in both groups; grade 3–4 toxicity rose from 8% to 24% with oxaliplatin. 24 In a second comparison, the intensified Capox50 regimen did not significantly increase pathological complete response (19.2% versus 13.9%; P=0.09) and added toxicity. Follow-up was short, and local-control and survival outcomes were not reported. 25 In the fluoropyrimidine comparison, capecitabine met the trial's equivalence rule against continuous-infusion fluorouracil as radiosensitiser; 3-year locoregional failure was 11.8% versus 11.2%. 26 NSABP R-04 oxaliplatin analysis: among 1,315 patients randomised after the amendment, oxaliplatin did not improve locoregional control, disease-free survival or overall survival. Worst grade 3–5 toxicity rose from about 27% to 41%, grade 3–5 diarrhoea from 6.9% to 16.5%, and fewer than 70% completed planned oxaliplatin. 26 NSABP R-04 safety signal: on-treatment or within-45-day deaths numbered 10 with capecitabine and 3 with fluorouracil across both protocol periods (nominal P=0.091), despite identical overall survival. This does not establish a fluoropyrimidine survival difference. 26 In the German oxaliplatin trial, 3-year disease-free survival was 75.9% versus 71.2% (HR 0.79; P=0.03) when oxaliplatin was incorporated into both chemoradiation and postoperative chemotherapy. The design cannot isolate a benefit from concurrent oxaliplatin alone. 27

records.title: Use total neoadjuvant therapy for selected disease
records.subtitle: Early rectal cancer · Colorectal
records.body: Use induction mFOLFIRINOX for a fit, locally advanced population The mFOLFIRINOX trial tested induction treatment: 2 Population: 461 patients with cT3 disease judged by a multidisciplinary team to warrant preoperative chemoradiation or cT4 M0 disease; performance status 0–1 and age under 76 years. Baseline stage was 81% cT3 and 18% cT4; nodal categories were N0 10%, N1 64% and N2 26%. Experimental regimen: mFOLFIRINOX every 2 weeks for six cycles, long-course chemoradiation with capecitabine 800 mg/m², TME, then 3 months of FOLFOX6 or capecitabine. Control: long-course chemoradiation, TME and 6 months of adjuvant chemotherapy. Protected result: 3-year disease-free survival was 75.7% versus 68.5%. Response: pathological complete response was 59/212 (27.8%) versus 26/215 (12.1%) among operated patients with evaluable pathology (reported as 28% versus 12%; P<0.0001). Long-term result: 7-year disease-free survival was 67.6% versus 62.5%, and 7-year overall survival 81.9% versus 76.1%. Limit: the long-term comparisons were nominal. Their P values, P=0.048 for disease-free survival and P=0.033 for overall survival, tested restricted-mean-survival-time differences rather than the displayed landmark rates. Distant control: 7-year metastasis-free survival was 79.2% versus 72.3%. Use short-course TNT with attention to local control RAPIDO tested short-course radiotherapy followed by chemotherapy: 1 Population: 920 patients with at least one MRI high-risk feature, including cT4 disease, cN2 disease, extramural vascular invasion, enlarged lateral nodes or mesorectal-fascia involvement. Experimental regimen: 5 × 5 Gy, then six 3-weekly CAPOX or nine 2-weekly FOLFOX cycles, approximately 4.5 months of neoadjuvant chemotherapy before TME, with no planned adjuvant chemotherapy. Control: long-course chemoradiation, TME and discretionary adjuvant chemotherapy, received by about half. Primary endpoint: disease-related treatment failure, defined as the first locoregional failure, distant metastasis, new colorectal primary or treatment-related death. Protected result: 3-year disease-related treatment failure was 23.7% versus 30.4% (HR 0.75; P=0.019); at 5 years it was 27.8% versus 34.0%. Response: pathological complete response was 120/423 (28%) versus 57/398 (14%) among resected patients (P<0.001). Distant control: distant metastasis at 5 years was 23.0% versus 30.4%. Randomised local-failure analysis: 5-year locoregional failure was 11.7% versus 8.1% (nominal P=0.07) in the eligible randomised population. Conditioned analysis: locoregional recurrence was 10.2% versus 6.1% (nominal P=0.027) among patients conditioned on R0/R1 resection, with two nonoperated standard-care progressors included. This is not a clean randomised comparison. Survival and limit: 5-year overall survival was 81.7% versus 80.2% at 5.6 years' median follow-up against a 10-year protocol. The schedule requires refinement for local control. Use the three-year STELLAR non-inferiority result at its tested scope STELLAR compared short-course TNT with long-course chemoradiation: 3 Population: 599 patients with distal or middle cT3–cT4 or node-positive rectal cancer. Experimental regimen: short-course radiotherapy, four 3-weekly CAPOX cycles, TME, then two CAPOX cycles. Control: long-course capecitabine chemoradiation, TME, then six 3-weekly CAPOX cycles. Three-year result: disease-free survival met the prespecified non-inferiority criterion (64.5% versus 62.3%; HR 0.883; one-sided 95% CI upper bound 1.11, below the 1.43 margin; P<0.001 for non-inferiority). Secondary outcomes: metastasis-free survival was 77.1% versus 75.3% (HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.63–1.24; nominal P=0.475). Locoregional recurrence was 8.4% versus 11.0% (HR 0.80, 95% CI 0.45–1.44; nominal P=0.461). Five-year result: disease-free survival was 62.0% versus 58.7%, and overall survival 78.1% versus 69.7%. Limit: the 5-year overall-survival comparison was nominal and unadjusted. The update did not restate or retest the non-inferiority margin, so the 3-year conclusion cannot be carried forward to 5 years. Post-hoc subgroup interactions do not establish risk-specific effects. Prefer consolidation sequencing when organ preservation is the objective The sequence trial compared TNT strategies: 28 Population: 311 patients with cT3/cT4 or node-positive rectal cancer. Regimen: induction FOLFOX followed by chemoradiation, or chemoradiation followed by consolidation FOLFOX. Design: a pick-the-winner phase II design against a 15% historical pathological-complete-response rate. Result: only the consolidation sequence met its prespecified hypothesis; pathological complete response was 25% versus 17%. Limit: the exploratory direct comparison was not conclusive (OR 1.69, 95% CI 0.96–2.99; P=0.071). Chemoradiation completion was better with consolidation sequencing, whereas systemic-chemotherapy completion was better with induction sequencing. Keep Polish II as historical high-risk TNT evidence Polish II 29 randomised 515 eligible patients with cT4 or fixed cT3 disease to 25 Gy in five fractions plus three FOLFOX4 cycles or 50.4 Gy chemoradiation containing bolus fluorouracil, leucovorin and oxaliplatin. At 8 years, OS was 49% in both groups; DFS was 43% versus 41% (HR 0.95, 95% CI 0.75–1.19). Local failure, distant metastasis and grade 3 or worse late complications did not significantly differ. The early OS difference disappeared, and superiority was not demonstrated. The oxaliplatin-containing control chemoradiation limits generalisability.

records.title: Omit pelvic radiation only in a selected population
records.subtitle: Early rectal cancer · Colorectal
records.body: Use response-directed mFOLFOX within PROSPECT eligibility PROSPECT was a 2023 randomised phase II/III non-inferiority trial: 4 Population: previously untreated cT2 node-positive or cT3 rectal adenocarcinoma judged by the patient's surgeon suitable for sphincter-sparing surgery. Exclusions: T4 disease, four or more pelvic nodes with short axis above 10 mm, and tumour within 3 mm of the radial margin. Low tumours: there was no numeric tumour-height exclusion. The surgeon-intent criterion filtered out low-lying tumours considered at high risk for incomplete resection, but 173/1,128 treated patients had tumours within 5 cm of the anal verge. Experimental regimen: six preoperative mFOLFOX6 cycles every 2 weeks, then TME after at least 20% tumour shrinkage. Chemoradiation triggers: less than 20% shrinkage (38/585), fewer than six FOLFOX cycles (8/585), or clinician/patient choice after randomisation (7/585). Radiation omission: 53/585 (9.1%) received preoperative chemoradiation; 90.9% avoided it before surgery. Control: chemoradiation to 50.4 Gy with a concurrent fluoropyrimidine, then TME. Postoperative treatment: six FOLFOX cycles after the experimental strategy and eight after control chemoradiation were recommended but not mandatory. Primary result: in the 1,128-patient per-protocol population, 5-year disease-free survival was 80.8% versus 78.6% (HR 0.92; two-sided 90.2% CI 0.74–1.14), meeting non-inferiority against the 1.29 margin. The all-1,194-randomised supplemental analysis was concordant. R0 resection: 90.4% versus 91.2% on the 585/543 per-protocol denominators; among 535/510 operated patients, R0 resection was 98.9% versus 97.1%. Pathological response: among operated patients, pathological complete response was 21.9% versus 24.3%. Local control: 5-year local recurrence was 1.8% versus 1.6% in the per-protocol population, an unadjusted secondary comparison. Overall survival: 5-year overall survival was 89.5% versus 90.2%; the trial was not designed for a definitive survival effect. Toxicity: chemotherapy caused more neuropathy and chemoradiation more diarrhoea. Limit: do not extrapolate to low tumours unsuitable for sphincter-sparing surgery or to the excluded high-risk groups. Do not generalise chemotherapy-only evidence CONVERT 30 randomised 663 patients with locally advanced tumours within 12 cm of the anal verge and uninvolved mesorectal fascia; 589 received four CAPOX cycles or capecitabine chemoradiation. Design and rescue: 300 received at least one CAPOX dose and 289 received chemoradiation. Local progression during CAPOX triggered chemoradiation before surgery; four patients used this rescue pathway. Two and five patients achieved a clinical complete response and used watch-and-wait. Operated population: 272 and 261 patients underwent TME. Pathological complete response was 30/272 (11.0%) versus 36/261 (13.8%), ypStage 0–1 downstaging 40.8% versus 45.6%, and R0 resection 99.6% in each group. These response/resection cells do not establish non-inferiority. Three-year locoregional-recurrence-free survival was 96.3% with CAPOX and 97.4% with chemoradiation (HR 1.40, 95% CI 0.53–3.68). Three-year DFS was 89.2% versus 87.9%, and OS 95.0% versus 94.1%. Non-inferiority was not confirmed. Acute haematological toxicity and lower grade 2–4 long-term adverse events are different endpoints; the latter favoured CAPOX. Chemotherapy alone remains a selected-patient option, not a universal substitute. FOWARC 31 randomised 495 stage II–III patients to fluorouracil-radiotherapy, mFOLFOX6-radiotherapy or mFOLFOX6 alone, followed by surgery and adjuvant chemotherapy. Original primary analysis: among 475 evaluable patients (155, 157 and 163 by arm), pathological complete response was 14.0%, 27.5% and 6.6%; R0 resection was 90.7%, 89.9% and 89.4%, respectively 32 . Ten-year DFS was 52.5%, 62.6% and 60.5% (P=.56). Ten-year local recurrence was 10.8%, 8.0% and 9.6% (P=.57); OS was 65.9%, 72.3% and 73.4% (P=.90). No arm significantly improved long-term disease control or survival. Do not extrapolate chemotherapy alone beyond carefully selected clear-margin disease.

records.title: Use watch-and-wait only with structured salvage capacity
records.subtitle: Early rectal cancer · Colorectal
records.body: Recognise the observational foundation The Habr-Gama cohort provided the initial observational evidence: 33 Population: 265 patients with distal rectal adenocarcinoma treated with fluorouracil/leucovorin chemoradiation to 5,040 cGy. The analysis compared 71 patients with a sustained clinical complete response against 22 patients found to have pT0N0M0 only after resection. Response gate: assessment at 8 weeks used clinical examination and endoscopy without MRI. The 71 observed patients had maintained complete regression for at least 12 months before inclusion in the observation group. Survival: 5-year overall survival was 100% observed versus 88% resected, with no cancer-related deaths among observed patients. Disease-free survival was 92% versus 83% and did not significantly differ. Recurrence: five of 71 observed patients recurred. Two bowel-wall recurrences at 56 and 64 months were salvaged and disease-free at last report; three patients developed systemic recurrence and none developed pelvic recurrence. Surgical cost: 16/22 resected patients received a stoma, including nine permanent colostomies. Limit: this was a single-institution observational comparison between outcome-defined groups, not a comparative efficacy trial. The IWWD registry provides multicentre estimates: 34 Population: 880 clinical complete responders from 47 centres. Regrowth: 2-year local regrowth was 25.2%; 97% arose in the bowel wall and 88% occurred within 2 years. Salvage: 101/115 documented salvage resections were R0; the authors estimated unsalvageable local disease at no more than 1% of the cohort. Distant disease: distant metastasis occurred in 8%. Survival: 5-year overall survival was 84.7% and disease-specific survival 93.8%. Outcome-defined comparison: overall survival was 87.9% with sustained response and 75.4% after regrowth; disease-specific survival after regrowth was 84.0%. No test between these groups was reported. Limit: there was no central response definition, and only 45% underwent the combined examination, endoscopy and MRI assessment recommended by the authors. Use consolidation sequencing to increase organ preservation OPRA tested the sequence of TNT, not watch-and-wait against a randomised surgery control: 5 Population: 324 patients with stage II disease (cT3–4N0) or stage III disease (any cT, N1–2). Baseline stage was 78% cT3, 15% cT4 and 7% cT1–2; 70% were node-positive and 30% node-negative. Sequences: induction chemotherapy followed by chemoradiation, or chemoradiation followed by consolidation chemotherapy. Chemotherapy was eight FOLFOX cycles or five CAPOX cycles. Restaging: within 8 weeks of TNT, use digital examination, endoscopy, pelvic MRI and CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis. Incomplete responders were directed to TME; complete and near-complete responders were offered watch-and-wait. Comparator: the primary disease-free-survival benchmark came from historical chemoradiation, TME and adjuvant chemotherapy. There was no concurrent randomised surgery-control arm. 2022 primary result: both sequences achieved 3-year disease-free survival of 76%, matching rather than exceeding the historical 75% benchmark. The primary endpoint was not met. 2022 organ preservation: 3-year organ preservation was 53% after chemoradiation-consolidation and 41% after induction-chemoradiation. 2022 regrowth: 75/225 watch-and-wait patients developed regrowth, 33% computed from the reported counts. Rates were 40% after induction-first and 27% after consolidation-first treatment. Later update: regrowth was 36%; 94% occurred within 2 years and 99% within 3 years. Later disease control: 5-year disease-free survival was 71% versus 69%. R0 resection after regrowth was 91% versus 90% after immediate TME for incomplete response, and 5-year disease-free survival was 64% in both groups. Later organ preservation: 5-year TME-free survival was 54% versus 39% (nominal P=0.012). Other secondary outcomes: 5-year overall survival was 88% versus 85%, locoregional-recurrence-free survival 94% versus 90%, and distant-metastasis-free survival 80% versus 78%. Treatment cost: grade 3 or higher toxicity was 41% versus 34%, with five treatment-related deaths. Limit: salvage and survival comparisons after regrowth are response-selected and based on few events. Consolidation sequencing increases the probability of organ preservation but does not establish survival superiority. Follow the OPRA protocol when applying its evidence The OPRA watch-and-wait protocol used: Digital rectal examination and flexible sigmoidoscopy every 4 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months for the next 3 years. Rectal MRI every 6 months for 2 years, then annually for 3 years. CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis at least annually. Biopsy of the primary site was not required by protocol. TME was recommended for feasible regrowth. 5

records.title: Discuss PD-1 blockade for dMMR rectal cancer
records.subtitle: Early rectal cancer · Colorectal
records.body: Define response with concordant examination, endoscopy and MRI In the dostarlimab programme, clinical complete response required no residual disease on digital examination, endoscopy and pelvic MRI. 6 Keep the single-arm evidence limit explicit The initial dostarlimab report described a single-arm phase 2 cohort of 16 previously untreated stage II–III dMMR rectal adenocarcinomas without distant metastases; 15 had stage III disease and one had stage II disease: 6 Lynch status: germline testing identified Lynch-associated pathogenic variants in 8/14 tested patients (57%). Regimen: dostarlimab 500 mg intravenously every 3 weeks for nine cycles over 6 months. Planned pathway: patients without a clinical complete response after dostarlimab were to receive chemoradiation to 50.4 Gy with capecitabine. Complete responders entered nonoperative follow-up; the remainder proceeded to TME. Interim result: all 12 patients who completed 6 months achieved a clinical complete response, and no enrolled patient received chemoradiation or surgery. Four patients remained on treatment. Maturity: median follow-up was 12 months from enrolment. Only four patients had maintained response for more than 1 year, and the sustained 12-month co-primary endpoint was not yet reported in finality. Safety: adverse events occurred in 12/16 patients (75%), with no grade 3 or higher event. The 2025 report expanded the programme: Rectal cohort: 50 patients were analysed and 49 completed dostarlimab. All 49 achieved a clinical complete response and chose nonoperative management. Durability: 37 had sustained response for at least 12 months, but the publication gives no denominator for that count. Recurrence-free survival: 2-year recurrence-free survival was 96% (95% CI 90–100) at median recurrence follow-up of 30.2 months. Pooled germline result: across rectal and nonrectal cohorts, 51/117 analysed patients (44%) had pathogenic germline mismatch-repair variants. This is not a rectal-only estimate. Limit: the evidence remains single-arm and does not establish replacement of standard local treatment for every patient with dMMR rectal cancer. 6

records.title: Adapt treatment to frailty, not age alone
records.subtitle: Early rectal cancer · Colorectal
records.body: Screen for frailty, functional reserve, comorbidity, cognition, nutrition and baseline neuropathy. Fit older adults should not be denied curative surgery or evidence-based neoadjuvant treatment solely because of age; frail patients need a multidisciplinary plan that prioritises function and treatment completion 35 . PRODIGE 23 enrolled performance-status 0–1 patients younger than 76 years, so its mFOLFIRINOX result should not be extrapolated automatically to a frail patient. ADORE's 55-patient subgroup aged 65 years or older was inconclusive, not evidence that oxaliplatin is ineffective; consider recurrence risk, neuropathy and competing mortality. When a frail patient still needs pelvic treatment, short-course radiotherapy or conventional fluoropyrimidine chemoradiation may reduce systemic intensity, but neither is intrinsically low burden. Surgery, postoperative chemotherapy and nonoperative management must remain feasible parts of the same plan.

records.title: Surveillance after curative treatment
records.subtitle: Early rectal cancer · Colorectal
records.body: After curative surgery, use CEA and CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis during the first 3 years. NICE specifies the modalities but not a universal visit-by-visit cadence; tailor frequency to stage, fitness for salvage treatment and local protocol. For pathological stage III disease after short-course or no preoperative radiotherapy, NICE lists CAPOX for 3 months, FOLFOX for 3–6 months or single-agent fluoropyrimidine for 6 months. Choose by histopathology, performance status, preferences, comorbidity and age; this is a postoperative pathway, not a substitute for appropriate TNT. Colonoscopy remains necessary after curative treatment, but NICE NG151 does not define its interval. Use the colorectal surveillance programme and shorten intervals for hereditary risk or polyp findings; do not invent a generic colonoscopy schedule from the rectal TNT trials. For watch-and-wait, use the OPRA schedule above when applying OPRA evidence. A clinical or radiological regrowth signal requires prompt multidisciplinary reassessment for salvage TME; the protocol does not support relaxed follow-up after an early complete response.
