records.title: At a glance
records.subtitle: Small cell lung cancer · Lung
records.body: Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) is managed as limited-stage or extensive-stage disease because the first treatment decision is whether definitive thoracic radiotherapy can be delivered safely within one tolerable field. Obtain contrast-enhanced chest and upper-abdominal imaging, brain MRI, and usually FDG-PET/CT before assigning stage; confirm any solitary finding that would change curative intent when feasible 1 . For fit limited-stage disease beyond a small node-negative tumour, use early concurrent platinum–etoposide and thoracic radiotherapy, then offer durvalumab when there has been no progression after concurrent chemoradiotherapy. For extensive-stage disease, use platinum–etoposide with atezolizumab or durvalumab when immunotherapy is suitable, followed by the corresponding maintenance strategy; reassess thoracic and intracranial disease before choosing consolidation. At relapse, treatment depends on the treatment-free interval, performance status, organ function, previous toxicity, and access. Tarlatamab improves survival over standard chemotherapy after platinum and now requires a step-up and monitored-start pathway; lurbinectedin, topotecan, platinum rechallenge, and selected single agents remain useful alternatives. Early palliative care and symptom-directed radiotherapy should accompany, not await failure of, systemic therapy.

records.title: Diagnosis, biology, and staging
records.subtitle: Small cell lung cancer · Lung
records.body: SCLC accounts for roughly 15% of lung cancers and is strongly associated with tobacco exposure. It is a high-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma with rapid proliferation, early dissemination, and frequent initial chemosensitivity followed by resistance. Central bulky disease, mediastinal adenopathy, cough, dyspnoea, weight loss, superior vena cava obstruction, and brain metastases are common clinical patterns. Paraneoplastic presentations include syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis, ectopic-ACTH Cushing syndrome, and Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome; hypercalcaemia is less characteristic than in non-small cell lung cancer. Common genomic abnormalities include TP53 mutation, RB1 loss, and MYC amplification, but none currently selects standard first-line treatment in de novo SCLC. Obtain adequate tissue for morphology and neuroendocrine immunophenotyping, while avoiding a nonessential invasive procedure that delays treatment in a clinically unstable patient. Routine broad molecular profiling does not select standard first-line therapy in de novo SCLC. Preserve tissue or plasma for a targeted question when mixed histology, an atypical clinical course, or transformation from a molecularly defined non-small cell cancer is suspected. Record both TNM stage and the practical two-stage category. Limited-stage disease is confined to one hemithorax with regional nodes that can be encompassed safely in a definitive radiation plan; extensive-stage disease exceeds that field or includes distant metastasis. Contralateral mediastinal or ipsilateral supraclavicular nodes may remain limited-stage, whereas malignant pleural or pericardial effusion generally defines extensive-stage disease 2 . Baseline assessment should include performance status, weight, full blood count, renal and hepatic function, electrolytes, and smoking status. Use brain MRI rather than CT when available. Consider pulmonary function testing before definitive thoracic radiotherapy, and assess hearing, neuropathy, and kidney function before cisplatin; carboplatin is reasonable when cisplatin toxicity would compromise treatment delivery.

records.title: Limited-stage disease
records.subtitle: Small cell lung cancer · Lung
records.body: Small node-negative tumours For clinical T1–2N0 disease, confirm mediastinal node negativity invasively when surgery is contemplated. In a fit patient with a resectable peripheral tumour, lobectomy with systematic nodal dissection followed by platinum–etoposide is an option; sublobar resection is generally inadequate. Unexpected nodal disease or a positive margin usually shifts postoperative management toward multidisciplinary chemoradiotherapy rather than surgery alone. Evidence supporting the surgical pathway Surgery is supported by retrospective selection rather than a modern randomized comparison. In 349 resected cases from the IASLC staging project, five-year survival was 48%, 39%, and 15% for pathological stages I, II, and III, respectively; these stage-conditioned outcomes cannot be compared directly with chemoradiotherapy series 3 . In a National Cancer Database analysis, surgery was associated with median survival of 38.6 versus 22.9 months for stage I disease, but residual confounding remains despite propensity matching. Among completely resected pT1–2N0 tumours, adjuvant therapy improved five-year survival from 40.4% to 52.7% in a separate observational cohort; these estimates support the pathway, not an individualized causal effect 4 5 . Stereotactic ablative radiotherapy followed by systemic therapy is a reasonable curative-intent alternative when a small node-negative tumour is medically inoperable, although randomized SCLC-specific evidence is limited. Do not extrapolate a surgery pathway to bulky or node-positive disease: most stage II–III limited-stage cancers are treated with definitive chemoradiotherapy because occult systemic disease is common even when imaging is apparently confined to the thorax. Stage II–III chemoradiotherapy Use four cycles of cisplatin–etoposide with thoracic radiotherapy starting during cycle 1 or 2 when tumour volume and organ-at-risk constraints permit. Carboplatin–etoposide is acceptable when cisplatin is unsuitable. Early multidisciplinary planning matters because postponing radiotherapy to complete chemotherapy can forfeit local control, while excessively large fields may require an individualized sequential approach to preserve safety. A common cisplatin–etoposide schedule is cisplatin 60–80 mg/m² on day 1 with etoposide 100–120 mg/m² on days 1–3 every three weeks; split cisplatin 25 mg/m² on days 1–3 can reduce hydration burden. Avoid unplanned early dose erosion where possible, but prioritize safe delivery and use current institutional protocols for renal, hepatic, marrow, and radiation-related adjustments. Choose the thoracic radiotherapy schedule Thoracic radiotherapy adds a modest but clinically meaningful survival benefit to chemotherapy. In an individual-patient meta-analysis of 2,103 analysable participants from 13 randomized trials, thoracic radiotherapy reduced the relative risk of death to 0.86 (95% CI 0.78–0.94; p=0.001) and increased three-year survival from 8.9% to 14.3%, an absolute gain of 5.4 percentage points 6 . Twice-daily radiotherapy remains the reference schedule for fit patients. In INT-0096, 45 Gy in 30 twice-daily fractions improved median overall survival from 19 to 23 months and five-year survival from 16% to 26% compared with 45 Gy once daily, at the cost of more grade 3 oesophagitis (27% versus 11%) 7 . CONVERT tested dose-escalated once-daily radiotherapy as a superiority strategy. Once-daily 66 Gy did not improve median overall survival over 45 Gy twice daily (25 versus 30 months; HR 1.18, 95% CI 0.95–1.45; p=0.14). This negative superiority result did not establish equivalence, but supports 66 Gy once daily as an alternative when twice-daily treatment is impractical 8 . Both twice-daily and once-daily guideline-concordant definitive schedules are used; select the schedule according to patient fitness, logistics, field size, organ-at-risk constraints and departmental expertise rather than treating one schedule as universally feasible 2 . Consolidation durvalumab Offer durvalumab to patients with stage I–III limited-stage SCLC, good performance status, and no progression after definitive concurrent platinum-based chemoradiotherapy, once acute toxicity has recovered. The current US regimen is 1,500 mg every four weeks until progression, unacceptable toxicity, or a maximum of 24 months; check the local label and contraindications before treatment 9 . Evidence for durvalumab In ADRIATIC, durvalumab improved median overall survival to 55.9 months versus 33.4 months with placebo (HR 0.73; 98.321% CI 0.54–0.98; p=0.01) and blinded independent-review progression-free survival to 16.6 versus 9.2 months (HR 0.76; 97.195% CI 0.59–0.98; p=0.02), crossing the prespecified interim boundaries 10 . Pneumonitis or radiation pneumonitis occurred in 38.2% with durvalumab and 30.2% with placebo; grade 3–4 events occurred in 3.1% and 2.6%, respectively, with one grade 5 event. Before starting treatment, distinguish resolving radiation injury from infection or immune pneumonitis. The tremelimumab comparison had not crossed its overall-survival boundary and does not establish a consolidation doublet. Atezolizumab does not establish a consolidation class effect Conference-abstract evidence does not establish a consolidation class effect. In ACHILES, one year of atezolizumab after concurrent chemoradiotherapy did not improve overall survival over observation (43.3 versus 38.8 months; HR 1.14, 95% CI 0.76–1.72; p=0.5) or secondary progression-free survival (21.1 versus 15.9 months; HR 0.88; nominal p=0.5). Grade 3–4 toxicity was 34% versus 20% and treatment-related deaths three versus none, but the one-page abstract did not report denominators, formal analysis-set definitions or complete safety detail 11 . Prophylactic cranial irradiation Discuss prophylactic cranial irradiation (PCI) after a good response to definitive treatment, especially in fit patients with stage II–III disease. In the individual-patient meta-analysis of 987 complete responders, PCI reduced mortality (RR 0.84; 95% CI 0.73–0.97; p=0.01), raised three-year survival from 15.3% to 20.7%, and reduced three-year brain-metastasis incidence from 58.6% to 33.3% 12 . The meta-analysis included only 140 patients with extensive-stage disease, and the stage interaction was not significant. Extensive-stage disease was imbalanced at baseline, 12% with PCI versus 17% without, driven by one component trial and no longer significant after trial adjustment. Neuropsychological testing was sparse, so the pooled evidence neither quantifies long-term cognitive harm nor excludes it. For an older, frail, or cognitively vulnerable patient, brain MRI surveillance is a reasonable alternative after shared decision-making. Explain fatigue, alopecia, memory effects, and the uncertainty around individual neurocognitive risk. The survival evidence arose from complete responders, whereas current recommendations often extend to broader responders; name that extrapolation during counselling rather than presenting the populations as identical.

records.title: Extensive-stage disease
records.subtitle: Small cell lung cancer · Lung
records.body: First-line systemic therapy For most fit patients, use carboplatin or cisplatin plus etoposide for four cycles with atezolizumab or durvalumab, followed by maintenance with the same checkpoint inhibitor. Do not delay urgent therapy for routine biomarker testing. Select the platinum according to renal function, hearing, neuropathy, emesis risk, marrow reserve, and the practical likelihood of completing treatment. Select the platinum Carboplatin and cisplatin have similar efficacy at a population level. In the COCIS individual-patient meta-analysis of 663 participants, median overall survival was 9.6 versus 9.4 months (HR 1.08; 95% CI 0.92–1.27; p=0.37), progression-free survival was 5.5 versus 5.3 months (HR 1.10; p=0.25), and response rates were 67.1% versus 66.0% 13 . Carboplatin caused more haematological toxicity and cisplatin more non-haematological toxicity in COCIS; 32% of participants had limited-stage disease. This supports toxicity-based platinum selection, not a claim that either drug is globally better tolerated. Etoposide is highly protein-bound and requires regimen-specific hepatic and renal review; avoid an automatic dose rule based on albumin alone. Place the cytotoxic backbone in context Historical randomized comparisons established platinum–etoposide as the cytotoxic backbone. In 437 eligible patients, etoposide–cisplatin, CAV and alternating CAV/EP produced similar median overall survival (8.6, 8.3 and 8.1 months; p=0.425); the trial was not designed to establish equivalence 14 . A Japanese mixed-stage trial likewise found no robust survival advantage for alternating CAV/PE over either regimen alone. The nominal alternating-versus-CAV comparison lost significance after prognostic adjustment, and stage-specific analyses were unpowered without an interaction test 15 . In the Norwegian trial, etoposide–cisplatin improved overall survival over CEV in 436 eligible patients (10.2 versus 7.8 months; one-sided p=0.0004). Limited- and extensive-stage results were descriptive because no treatment-by-stage interaction was reported 16 . Add a survival-positive checkpoint inhibitor In IMpower133, atezolizumab plus carboplatin–etoposide improved median overall survival from 10.3 to 12.3 months (HR 0.70; 95% CI 0.54–0.91; p=0.007) and progression-free survival from 4.3 to 5.2 months (HR 0.77; p=0.02). Confirmed response rates were similar in a post-hoc analysis (60.2% versus 64.4%); this analysis does not identify the mechanism of the survival benefit 17 . In CASPIAN, durvalumab plus platinum–etoposide improved median overall survival from 10.3 to 13.0 months at the primary interim analysis (HR 0.73; 95% CI 0.59–0.91; p=0.0047); the updated comparison was 12.9 versus 10.5 months (HR 0.75; 95% CI 0.62–0.91; nominal p=0.0032). The trial permitted cisplatin and did not use maintenance etoposide 18 . At the primary interim analysis, CASPIAN progression-free survival was 5.1 versus 5.4 months (HR 0.78), and confirmed response was 68% versus 58%; these were not alpha-protected efficacy claims in the reported hierarchy and should remain secondary context. In IMpower133, treatment-related grade 3–4 events occurred in 56.6% versus 56.1%, and immune-mediated adverse events in 39.9% versus 24.5%. Do not add tremelimumab routinely: the CASPIAN durvalumab–tremelimumab arm did not cross its prespecified overall-survival boundary. Pembrolizumab improved progression-free survival in KEYNOTE-604 (4.5 versus 4.3 months; HR 0.75; p=0.0023) but its overall-survival result (10.8 versus 9.7 months; HR 0.80; p=0.0164) missed the multiplicity-adjusted boundary of p=0.0128 19 . At 12 months, progression-free survival in KEYNOTE-604 was 13.6% versus 3.1%; response was 70.6% versus 61.8%, an exploratory comparison. Grade 3–4 adverse events occurred in 76.7% and 74.9%. These secondary signals do not reverse the failed overall-survival hypothesis and should not be used to promote pembrolizumab over an approved survival-positive first-line regimen. Consider regional and selected alternatives Serplulimab plus chemotherapy improved median overall survival to 15.4 months versus 10.9 months in ASTRUM-005 (HR 0.63; 95% CI 0.49–0.82; p<0.001). The enrolled population was predominantly Asian, 68.4% were Chinese, there were no US sites, and non-Asian follow-up was short; use must follow local approval and access rather than cross-trial efficacy ranking 20 . Blinded-review progression-free survival was 5.7 versus 4.3 months (HR 0.48), and response was 80.2% versus 70.4%, but these were exploratory and no formal PFS p-value was reported. Treatment-related grade 3 or higher adverse events occurred in 33.2% versus 27.6%; immune-related events occurred in 37.0% versus 18.4%, with study-drug deaths in 0.8% versus 0.5%. Other chemo-immunotherapy regimens may be approved regionally. In EXTENTORCH, toripalimab improved median overall survival to 14.6 versus 13.3 months (HR 0.80; p=0.03) and progression-free survival (HR 0.67; p<0.001) 21 . CAPSTONE-1 reported 15.3 versus 12.8 months with adebrelimab (HR 0.72; p=0.0017); neither comparison establishes superiority over atezolizumab or durvalumab 22 . Irinotecan–cisplatin produced longer survival than etoposide–cisplatin in the Japanese JCOG9511 trial: 12.8 versus 9.4 months (relative risk of death 0.60; 95% CI 0.43–0.83; p=0.002). Progression-free survival was 6.9 versus 4.8 months, and response was 84.4% versus 67.5%; these secondary comparisons were nominal 23 . The JCOG9511 result was not consistently reproduced outside Japan. Severe diarrhoea occurred in 16% versus 0%, while neutropenia was less frequent; three versus one treatment-related deaths occurred. These efficacy and toxicity patterns make irinotecan–cisplatin an alternative in selected settings rather than a universal first-line standard. Immediate complications and supportive care Treat symptomatic brain metastases according to neurological urgency, number and volume of lesions, extracranial control, and performance status; do not reflexively substitute PCI for therapeutic brain radiotherapy. Give corticosteroids for clinically significant oedema and involve radiation oncology early. Seizure prophylaxis is not routine without a seizure, while anticonvulsant treatment is indicated after one occurs. Bulky, highly chemosensitive SCLC can cause tumour lysis syndrome, particularly with renal impairment, elevated urate, high lactate dehydrogenase, or extensive liver involvement. Correct electrolytes and dehydration, stratify risk before chemotherapy, use urate-lowering prophylaxis when appropriate, and monitor closely during the first treatment cycle rather than assuming solid tumours carry no lysis risk 24 . Superior vena cava obstruction requires rapid assessment of airway, cerebral, and haemodynamic compromise. Obtain tissue first when safely possible, but do not delay stenting or other urgent stabilization in life-threatening obstruction. Systemic therapy often relieves SCLC-related obstruction promptly; radiotherapy and endovascular stenting are complementary options selected by severity, prior treatment, and expected speed of response 25 . Maintenance after induction Continue atezolizumab or durvalumab after first-line chemo-immunotherapy when disease is controlled and toxicity is acceptable. For patients treated with atezolizumab plus carboplatin–etoposide, maintenance lurbinectedin plus atezolizumab is an additional option after four induction cycles, provided there is no progression and the patient can tolerate increased marrow toxicity. Evidence for lurbinectedin plus atezolizumab In IMforte, 483 induction responders were rerandomized at maintenance. Lurbinectedin plus atezolizumab improved median progression-free survival from maintenance randomization from 2.1 to 5.4 months (HR 0.54; 95% CI 0.43–0.67; p<0.0001) and interim overall survival from 10.6 to 13.2 months (HR 0.73; 95% CI 0.57–0.95; p=0.017), crossing both prespecified boundaries 26 . Grade 3–4 all-cause adverse events occurred in 38% with the combination and 22% with atezolizumab alone; treatment-related grade 3–4 events occurred in 26% and 6%. Response from maintenance randomization was 19% versus 10%, and patients with brain metastases were excluded. The regimen received US approval in 2025 27 . Do not extrapolate across maintenance strategies Verify the current label, blood-count thresholds, dose modifications, and local access before prescribing rather than carrying induction lurbinectedin dosing into maintenance by assumption. Choosing durvalumab for first-line treatment also precludes direct extrapolation of IMforte, because the trial required atezolizumab-based induction and randomized only patients without progression after induction. Do not substitute nivolumab-based maintenance. CheckMate 451 did not improve its primary overall-survival endpoint with nivolumab plus ipilimumab versus placebo (9.2 versus 9.6 months; HR 0.92; p=0.37). The fixed hierarchy then stopped, so nivolumab overall survival and both progression-free-survival comparisons were not formally tested. Grade 3–4 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 52.2%, 11.5% and 8.4% with the combination, nivolumab and placebo 28 . Thoracic radiotherapy after systemic therapy Evidence before checkpoint inhibition Post-chemotherapy thoracic radiotherapy is not routine for every patient. In 498 CREST participants, 30 Gy in 10 fractions after chemotherapy and PCI did not significantly improve the primary one-year overall-survival endpoint: 33% versus 28% (HR 0.84; 95% CI 0.69–1.01; p=0.066). The nominal secondary two-year survival rates were 13% versus 3% 29 . CREST progression-free survival was 4 versus 3 months (HR 0.73; 95% CI 0.61–0.87; nominal p=0.001), with six-month rates of 24% versus 20%. These secondary results support a local-control discussion in selected responders but cannot repair the missed primary one-year overall-survival endpoint. Evidence with atezolizumab maintenance The randomized evidence predates first-line checkpoint inhibition. In the phase II TREASURE trial during atezolizumab maintenance, thoracic radiotherapy did not improve progression-free or overall survival and increased serious adverse events (61.3% versus 18.2%) and fatal events (19.4% versus 3.0%); early closure made efficacy estimates imprecise but argues against routine unselected use with atezolizumab maintenance 30 . Select patients narrowly Consider consolidative thoracic radiotherapy only after multidisciplinary review for a fit responder with limited residual thoracic burden, controlled extracranial disease, and acceptable lung and oesophageal constraints. The historical Jeremic trial enrolled 206 highly selected patients with an extrathoracic complete response and at least an intrathoracic partial response after three platinum–etoposide cycles; do not generalize its intensive regimen broadly 31 . PCI or MRI surveillance Evidence without mandated baseline MRI For extensive-stage responders, choose between PCI and scheduled brain MRI surveillance through shared decision-making. In 286 EORTC 08993-22993 participants, baseline brain imaging was not mandatory; PCI reduced symptomatic brain metastases (16.8% versus 41.3%; HR 0.27; 95% CI 0.16–0.44; p<0.001) and one-year incidence from 40.4% to 14.6% 32 . EORTC median overall survival was 6.7 versus 5.4 months (HR 0.68; 95% CI 0.52–0.88; nominal p=0.003), with one-year survival of 27.1% versus 13.3%. Because overall survival was secondary and occult baseline brain metastases could have been treated by PCI, the result does not directly answer the modern MRI-negative surveillance question. Evidence with MRI surveillance In the Japanese MRI-surveillance trial, 224 participants had no brain metastases on mandated baseline MRI and underwent MRI every three months in year 1 and at months 18 and 24. PCI did not improve median overall survival (11.6 versus 13.7 months; HR 1.27; 95% CI 0.96–1.68; p=0.094) 33 . The 12-month cumulative incidence of brain metastases was 32.9% with PCI versus 59.0% with observation, while progression-free survival was 2.3 versus 2.4 months (HR 0.98; p=0.75). Salvage brain radiotherapy was used in 46% versus 83%. Attrition in cognitive testing prevents a claim of neurocognitive equivalence. These trials answer different questions: PCI remains reasonable when reliable MRI surveillance or prompt salvage treatment is unavailable, or when a patient prioritizes reducing intracranial relapse. MRI surveillance is reasonable when high-quality follow-up is dependable or cognitive risk is a major concern. The MAVERICK trial is closed to accrual, and no practice-changing primary result has been reported 34 .

records.title: Relapsed or refractory disease
records.subtitle: Small cell lung cancer · Lung
records.body: Reassess before choosing treatment Confirm progression and distinguish it from infection, radiation change, immune toxicity, or a second primary cancer. Refractory disease never responded to first-line therapy; resistant relapse occurs within three months, sensitive relapse after three months, and late relapse after six months. Use the exact interval from the last platinum dose rather than the label alone when selecting treatment. Prioritize a clinical trial whenever available. For rapidly symptomatic disease, choose a regimen that can start promptly and is deliverable with existing marrow, renal, hepatic, and neurological reserve. Re-biopsy is not routine for typical recurrent de novo SCLC, but it is important when pathology was uncertain, behaviour is atypical, or transformed disease would change a molecularly guided non-small cell pathway. Tarlatamab Randomized evidence Tarlatamab is a DLL3-directed bispecific T-cell engager for extensive-stage SCLC progressing on or after platinum. In DeLLphi-304, it improved median overall survival to 13.6 months versus 8.3 months with physician-selected chemotherapy (HR 0.60; 95% CI 0.47–0.77; p<0.001). Twelve-month restricted mean progression-free survival was 5.3 versus 4.3 months; proportional-hazards assumptions were not satisfied 35 . DeLLphi-304 response was 35% versus 20% (relative risk 1.73), median response duration 6.9 versus 5.5 months, and 12-month response durability 41% versus 13%. Grade 3 or higher treatment-related events occurred in 27% versus 62%. Cytokine-release syndrome occurred in 56% with tarlatamab, including 1% grade 3, and ICANS in 6%, with one grade 5 event. Patient-reported chest-pain improvement did not meet the prespecified hierarchy, so physical functioning and global health were not formally tested. That failed hierarchy should temper symptom-benefit claims even though survival and comparative toxicity favoured tarlatamab in this otherwise survival-positive randomized comparison. Earlier single-arm evidence The earlier DeLLphi-301 selected-dose cohort showed a blinded independent-review response rate of 40% among 100 patients (97.5% CI 29%–52%) after platinum and at least one additional line. Median progression-free survival was 4.9 months and overall survival was immature at 14.3 months. Cytokine-release syndrome occurred in 51% at 10 mg, mostly low grade 36 . At 10 mg, grade 3 cytokine-release syndrome occurred in 1% and ICANS in 8%, without a grade 3 or higher ICANS event. Overall grade 3 or higher adverse events occurred in 59% of the 133-patient safety population, and one treatment-related respiratory-failure death occurred. These uncontrolled dose-expansion results establish activity and safety context, not comparative efficacy. Deliver tarlatamab safely Use the current label rather than the trial-era monitoring schedule: 1 mg on cycle 1 day 1, then 10 mg on days 8 and 15 and every two weeks thereafter. After cycle 1 days 1 and 8, monitor in an appropriate healthcare setting for 22–24 hours and require the patient to remain within one hour of care for 48 hours with a caregiver 37 . Cytokine-release syndrome and neurological toxicity, including ICANS, can be severe or fatal. Give label-specified premedication and hydration, ensure tocilizumab and emergency support are available, and establish a caregiver and proximity plan before the first dose. Later monitoring can be reduced only according to the current label and prior reaction history, not by assuming cycle 1 tolerance. Lurbinectedin, topotecan, and other chemotherapy Lurbinectedin Lurbinectedin is an option after platinum, especially when an outpatient every-three-week regimen is desirable. In the phase II PM1183-B-005 basket cohort, investigator-assessed response was 35.2% (37/105; 95% CI 26.2%–45.2%), median progression-free survival was 3.5 months, and median overall survival was 9.3 months. Grade 3–4 neutropenia occurred in 46% and febrile neutropenia in 5% 38 . Median response duration was 6.2 months when the chemotherapy-free interval was at least 90 days and 4.7 months when shorter; response rates were 45.0% and 22.2%. These were nonrandomized subgroup descriptions without a reported interaction, so the interval informs selection but does not prove differential treatment effect. Dose according to the current product information and adjust for hepatic function, cytopenias, and interacting medicines. Maintain vigilance for myelosuppression, hepatotoxicity, extravasation injury, and rhabdomyolysis 39 . Topotecan and selected single agents Intravenous topotecan and cyclophosphamide–doxorubicin–vincristine had comparable activity in a randomized trial: response rates were 24.3% and 18.3% (p=0.285), time to progression 13.3 and 12.3 weeks (p=0.552), response duration 14.4 and 15.3 weeks (p=0.300), and survival 25.0 and 24.7 weeks (p=0.795) 40 . Both regimens require careful marrow monitoring. Seven treatment-related deaths from sepsis or myelosuppression occurred in the trial, and the reported symptom improvements were nominal analyses using nonvalidated measures. Topotecan commonly causes severe neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, and anaemia; do not interpret similar median survival as equivalent tolerability. Oral topotecan prolonged median survival to 26 versus 14 weeks compared with best supportive care in patients unsuitable for intravenous treatment (p=0.0104), with a 7% response rate and 44% stable disease. In sensitive relapse, oral and intravenous topotecan produced median survival of 33 and 35 weeks and response rates of 18% and 22% 41 42 . Use the locally licensed formulation and renal dose adjustments. Other selected options include irinotecan, paclitaxel, temozolomide, gemcitabine, or vinorelbine, but evidence is generally noncomparative and choice should be individualized. The small irinotecan studies span heterogeneous populations and do not support a single pooled response estimate; vinorelbine access requirements depend on the formulation and local infusion practice. Platinum rechallenge For platinum-sensitive relapse, platinum–etoposide rechallenge is reasonable. In JCOG0605, 180 highly selected participants relapsing at least 90 days after platinum were randomized to cisplatin–etoposide–irinotecan or topotecan; median overall survival was 18.2 versus 12.5 months (HR 0.67; 90% CI 0.51–0.88; p=0.0079) 43 . The JCOG0605 experimental regimen used cisplatin on days 1 and 8, etoposide on days 1–3, irinotecan on day 8, and prophylactic G-CSF in a two-week schedule for five cycles. Its intensity and substantial toxicity limit generalizability; do not substitute this triplet automatically for a conventional platinum–etoposide rechallenge in a frail patient. GFPC 01-13 directly supports a simpler rechallenge strategy after a response and relapse at least 90 days from first-line platinum–etoposide. Carboplatin–etoposide improved centrally reviewed progression-free survival over oral topotecan (4.7 versus 2.7 months; HR 0.57, 90% CI 0.41–0.73; one-sided p=0.0041), but exploratory overall survival was unchanged (7.5 versus 7.4 months; HR 1.03; nominal p=0.94) 44 . Investigational antibody–drug conjugates Izalontamab brengitecan is an EGFR–HER3 bispecific antibody–drug conjugate with exploratory activity in relapsed extensive-stage disease. In a 52-patient single-arm phase Ib cohort, response was 48.1%, median response duration 4.9 months and median overall survival 12.2 months. The unplanned second-line subgroup response was 72.7%, but no comparator or formal hypothesis test supports a comparative claim 45 . Toxicity and uncertainty currently preclude routine use. Grade 3 or higher treatment-related adverse events occurred in 75%, serious treatment-related events in 50%, dose reduction in 46.2%, treatment delay in 63.5%, and treatment-related death in two of 52 patients. Use should remain within a clinical trial or another governed investigational pathway.

records.title: Follow-up and survivorship
records.subtitle: Small cell lung cancer · Lung
records.body: After curative-intent treatment, use clinical review and contrast-enhanced chest imaging about every three months in year 1, every six months in years 2–3, and then less frequently according to risk and fitness for salvage. After extensive-stage treatment, tailor imaging to active therapy and symptoms. Investigate new focal or neurological symptoms immediately rather than waiting for the next surveillance scan 46 . For patients who do not receive PCI, obtain brain MRI every three months in the first year and every six months in the second year, with further imaging individualized. Surveillance imaging should be offered only when detection could lead to meaningful treatment. Continue smoking-cessation support, vaccination, pulmonary rehabilitation when appropriate, nutritional care, and assessment for hearing, neuropathy, cognition, mood, and treatment-related cardiopulmonary effects 47 . At every transition, document goals of care and the threshold for stopping disease-directed treatment. SCLC can change quickly, so provide clear contact instructions for new dyspnoea, haemoptysis, confusion, weakness, severe headache, fever, or uncontrolled pain. Integrate palliative care early, and revisit resuscitation preferences before an acute crisis rather than equating symptom care with treatment withdrawal.

records.title: Establish the diagnosis and treatment-defining biology
records.subtitle: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma · Lymphoma
records.body: DLBCL is biologically heterogeneous. Gene-expression profiling separated germinal-centre B-cell-like (GCB) from activated B-cell-like (ABC) disease, and this division tracked survival after anthracycline-based chemotherapy. The foundational analysis included 40 patients with survival data and was exploratory: 5-year survival was 76% versus 16% (nominal p=0.01), with no hazard ratio or multivariable model. Alizadeh et al. (Lymphochip) Cell of origin may be reported by an immunohistochemical classifier, but it should not select frontline treatment. Trials that prospectively enriched for non-GCB or ABC disease have not established a cell-of-origin-directed standard. Before treatment: Rebiopsy at each relapse, where feasible, to confirm DLBCL. 2 Perform PET-CT for staging. Record the IPI or age-adjusted IPI; calculate the CNS-IPI when CNS prophylaxis is being considered. ESMO Lymphomas Guideline (Eyre et al.) Test for a MYC rearrangement by FISH. If MYC is rearranged, add BCL2 FISH; MYC/BCL2 protein co-expression is not the definition of double-hit lymphoma. 2 Obtain a baseline ECG. Echocardiography is recommended for older patients and those with cardiovascular risk factors and may be considered for all patients. 2

records.title: Stage and assess response with PET-CT
records.subtitle: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma · Lymphoma
records.body: PET-CT is the standard baseline and response-assessment modality. Interim PET-CT can be considered when it will change a prespecified treatment pathway. 2 Use the same response framework that governs the treatment pathway. A Deauville score of 1–3 defines complete metabolic response in the current limited-stage PET-adapted algorithm; a score of 4–5 after two cycles directs the longer chemotherapy and radiotherapy branch. 2

records.title: Use prognostic scores to structure risk, not to replace judgement
records.subtitle: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma · Lymphoma
records.body: The IPI and age-adjusted IPI remain the principal outcome-stratification scores. They also define current first-line branches: IPI 0–1 supports R-CHOP, whereas IPI 2 or higher permits pola-R-CHP as an alternative in fit patients younger than 80. The CNS-IPI informs discussion of CNS staging and prophylaxis, but does not prove that prophylaxis is effective. 2

records.title: Prevent early treatment complications
records.subtitle: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma · Lymphoma
records.body: Tumour lysis syndrome Assess tumour lysis risk before treatment. Use the active institutional protocol for biochemical monitoring, hydration, urate-lowering therapy, G6PD testing before rasburicase, electrolyte management and dialysis escalation. R-CHOP delivery R-CHOP should be prescribed from the active institutional protocol, including dose caps, infusion precautions, hepatitis B management, growth-factor policy and anti-infective prophylaxis.

records.title: Choose first-line treatment by stage, IPI, age and fitness
records.subtitle: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma · Lymphoma
records.body: Limited-stage disease For fit patients younger than 60 with IPI 0 and non-bulky disease below 7.5 cm, give four cycles of R-CHOP followed by two further rituximab doses. The same approach can be considered at age 60–80 when there are no additional risk factors. 2 FLYER directly supports chemotherapy de-escalation in this narrow population. Four cycles of R-CHOP plus two further rituximab doses were non-inferior to six R-CHOP cycles for 3-year PFS (96% vs 94%), with fewer non-haematological adverse events. Both groups received six rituximab doses. The endpoint changed from EFS to PFS after the first interim analysis, and superiority was not tested. For fit patients younger than 80 with limited-stage bulky disease and aaIPI 0, use PET after two cycles. Complete metabolic response permits four total cycles of R-CHOP without further rituximab; Deauville 4–5 directs six cycles followed by involved-site radiotherapy. 2 For limited-stage aaIPI 1 or higher, options are six cycles of R-CHOP, six cycles of pola-R-CHP when IPI is 2 or higher, or three to four cycles of R-CHOP followed by involved-site radiotherapy. Patients aged 80 or older should generally receive six cycles of R-miniCHOP. 2 MInT established the value of rituximab in younger good-prognosis disease rather than the abbreviated regimen itself. Adding rituximab to six cycles of CHOP-like chemotherapy improved 3-year EFS from 59% to 79% and 3-year OS from 84% to 93%. The trial stopped early at its first interim analysis, and the often-cited HR 0.44 was derived from a multivariable model. Advanced-stage disease For fit patients younger than 80, use six cycles of R-CHOP for IPI 0–1. Six cycles of pola-R-CHP is a first-line option for IPI 2 or higher. 2 LNH-98.5 (GELA) established rituximab with CHOP in patients aged 60–80. The prespecified 2-year analysis showed better EFS (57% vs 38%, p<0.001) and OS (70% vs 57%, p=0.007); the benefit persisted at 5 years (OS 58% vs 45%). The primary report found no clinically meaningful increase in toxicity. RICOVER-60 compared six or eight cycles of CHOP-14 with or without rituximab in patients aged 61–80. Rituximab drove the benefit. Six cycles of R-CHOP-14 improved 3-year OS over six CHOP-14 cycles (78.1% vs 67.7%), whereas adding cycles 7 and 8 did not improve outcome and increased treatment-associated deaths. Dose-dense scheduling did not improve survival. In R-CHOP-14 v 21 (NCRI) , 2-year OS was 82.7% with R-CHOP-14 and 80.8% with R-CHOP-21 (HR 0.90, 95% CI 0.70–1.15); PFS also did not differ. Treatment-related deaths were numerically higher with the 14-day schedule (9 vs 3), without statistical significance. Pola-R-CHP POLARIX replaced vincristine with polatuzumab vedotin in 879 previously untreated patients aged 18–80 with IPI 2–5. The primary PFS endpoint was met at 2 years (76.7% vs 70.2%; HR 0.73, 95% CI 0.57–0.95; p=0.02), and the advantage persisted at 5 years (64.9% vs 59.1%; HR 0.77, 0.62–0.97). No statistically significant OS advantage had been demonstrated at the 5-year analysis (82.3% vs 79.5%; HR 0.85, 95% CI 0.63–1.15). Fewer patients required subsequent therapy over 5 years (25.5% vs 35.3%). Grade 3 or higher adverse events were similar overall, although grade 3–4 febrile neutropenia was more frequent with pola-R-CHP (13.8% vs 8.0%). Do not use the exploratory cell-of-origin results to select pola-R-CHP. The 5-year PFS estimates favoured treatment in ABC disease (HR 0.38) but not GCB disease (HR 1.07); no interaction test was reported. New R-CHOP combinations frontMIND added tafasitamab and lenalidomide to R-CHOP in high-risk untreated DLBCL or high-grade B-cell lymphoma. PFS improved (HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.59–0.96; 2-year 71.1% vs 62.9%), but interim OS was not significant and remained immature (HR 0.85, 0.63–1.14). Grade 3 or higher treatment-emergent events increased from 76% to 87%. DEB enrolled patients with MYC/BCL2 double-expressor DLBCL and excluded double-hit or triple-hit disease. Tucidinostat plus R-CHOP improved 2-year EFS (60.3% vs 50.5%; HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.54–0.96), but PFS, OS and DFS intervals crossed 1. Toxicity increased, particularly during tucidinostat maintenance, and the trial was conducted entirely in China. These regimens improve surrogate endpoints in selected populations without a demonstrated OS advantage to date. They should not be presented as interchangeable with R-CHOP or pola-R-CHP.

records.title: Recognise the limits of frontline intensification
records.subtitle: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma · Lymphoma
records.body: Several phase 3 strategies failed on their primary endpoint: CALGB/Alliance 50303 found no PFS or OS advantage for DA-EPOCH-R over R-CHOP (PFS HR 0.93, p=0.65; OS HR 1.09, p=0.64). Grade 3–5 treatment-related events occurred in 98% versus 78%, with more febrile neutropenia, neuropathy and mucositis. GOYA found no PFS benefit from substituting obinutuzumab for rituximab (3-year 69.6% vs 66.9%; HR 0.92, p=0.39), with more grade 3–5, serious and fatal adverse events. REMoDL-B found no primary PFS benefit from adding bortezomib to R-CHOP (30-month HR 0.86, p=0.28). A nominal 5-year treatment-by-cell-of-origin interaction remains hypothesis-generating; grade 3 or higher neuropathy and serious adverse events were more frequent with bortezomib. PHOENIX missed both co-primary EFS endpoints with ibrutinib-R-CHOP. The exploratory age interaction suggested benefit below 60 and numerical harm at 60 or older, alongside greater toxicity and reduced delivery of R-CHOP in older patients. ROBUST found no PFS improvement from lenalidomide-R-CHOP in prospectively selected ABC disease (HR 0.85, p=0.29), with more haematological toxicity and treatment discontinuation. SWOG 9704 tested upfront autologous transplant in high-intermediate- or high-risk responders after induction. Transplant improved one co-primary endpoint, 2-year PFS (69% vs 55%; p=0.005), but not OS (74% vs 71%; p=0.30). Only 150 of 225 randomised patients with B-cell lymphoma received rituximab. Upfront transplant is not routine first-remission consolidation.

records.title: Select CNS prophylaxis sparingly
records.subtitle: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma · Lymphoma
records.body: High CNS relapse risk and prophylaxis efficacy are different questions. Calculate the CNS-IPI when prophylaxis is under consideration. End-of-treatment high-dose methotrexate, two cycles of 3–3.5 g/m², may be considered only for highly selected younger patients at ultra-high risk, such as CNS-IPI 5–6, multiple extranodal sites, or renal, adrenal, breast or testicular involvement. The recommendation is weak [IV,C]. 2 Lewis (International CNS Prophylaxis Study Group) analysed 2,418 high-risk patients, 425 of whom received high-dose methotrexate. The diagnosis-time analysis favoured prophylaxis but was vulnerable to immortal-time bias. In 1,616 patients in complete response after induction, high-dose methotrexate was not associated with lower CNS progression (adjusted HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.4–1.3; p=0.30; adjusted 5-year risk 5.0% vs 6.5%).

records.title: Use radiotherapy selectively
records.subtitle: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma · Lymphoma
records.body: Consider involved-site radiotherapy with a radiation oncologist for an initial isolated bulky lesion of at least 7 cm or a residual FDG-avid area suspicious for disease when biopsy is not feasible. Residual FDG-avid lesions should be biopsied wherever feasible. 2 This is a case-by-case decision. Routine consolidation after a complete metabolic response is not established in the PET-CT era.

records.title: Adapt treatment for older or anthracycline-unfit patients
records.subtitle: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma · Lymphoma
records.body: Use comprehensive geriatric and organ-function assessment rather than chronological age alone. Patients aged 80 or older can receive six cycles of R-miniCHOP; full-dose R-CHOP may be considered only in exceptionally fit individuals. A corticosteroid pre-phase or first-cycle cytotoxic attenuation can be considered when disease burden causes reversible physiological impairment. 2 LNH03-7B (R-miniCHOP) studied 150 patients older than 80. R-miniCHOP used full-dose rituximab with attenuated cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin and vincristine. Median OS was 29 months, 2-year OS 59% and 2-year PFS 47%. Treatment remained hazardous: 18% died during treatment and 12 deaths were attributed to treatment toxicity. The study was single-arm. When anthracycline is unsuitable, guideline-supported options include six cycles of R-CEOP, R-COMP or R-GCVP. Regimen choice should reflect cardiac function, comorbidity, disease tempo and local protocol. 2

records.title: Manage double-hit and double-expressor disease separately
records.subtitle: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma · Lymphoma
records.body: MYC/BCL2 double-hit lymphoma is defined by rearrangements, whereas double-expressor DLBCL is defined by protein expression. For young, fit patients with co-existing MYC and BCL2 rearrangements, treatment intensification with DA-EPOCH-R or R-CODOX-M/R-IVAC can be considered, but the recommendation rests on low-level evidence. 2 The negative unselected DA-EPOCH-R comparison does not resolve the optimal regimen for double-hit lymphoma. Conversely, the DEB result applies to double-expressor disease and excluded double-hit or triple-hit disease. Do not transfer either result across these biological groups.

records.title: Reassess disease at relapse
records.subtitle: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma · Lymphoma
records.body: Rebiopsy at relapse where feasible. Define treatment by time from first-line therapy, suitability for CAR T-cell therapy or transplant, prior exposures, organ function and the feasibility of delivering treatment without disease progression during manufacture. 2 SCHOLAR-1 provides the pre-CAR-T benchmark for refractory large B-cell lymphoma: ORR 26%, CR 7%, median OS 6.3 months and 20% alive at 2 years. It pooled two trials and two institutional cohorts without central response review, and should not be treated as a randomised comparator. Refractory disease or relapse within 12 months For suitable patients, second-line anti-CD19 CAR T-cell therapy with axicabtagene ciloleucel or lisocabtagene maraleucel is preferred. 2 ZUMA-7 improved EFS over platinum salvage followed by transplant in responders (median 8.3 vs 2.0 months; HR 0.40; 24-month 41% vs 16%). ORR was 83% versus 50% and CR 65% versus 32%. Interim OS did not reach significance (HR 0.73, 95% CI 0.53–1.01), with 56% of controls later receiving cellular therapy. TRANSFORM improved EFS with lisocabtagene maraleucel (median 10.1 vs 2.3 months; HR 0.35), with CR 66% versus 39%. Interim OS was immature (HR 0.51, 95% CI 0.26–1.00), and 50 of 92 controls were approved to cross over. BELINDA found no EFS benefit with tisagenlecleucel (median 3.0 months in both groups; HR 1.07). Median time from leukapheresis to infusion was 52 days; 83% received bridging therapy and 26% had progressed by the week-6 assessment before infusion. Product delivery matters, and lymphodepletion is regimen-specific. ZUMA-7 used cyclophosphamide 500 mg/m² plus fludarabine 30 mg/m² daily on days −5 to −3. 20 TRANSFORM used cyclophosphamide 300 mg/m² plus fludarabine 30 mg/m² daily for three days. 21 Later relapse in transplant-suitable patients For relapse beyond 12 months, use platinum-based reinduction and proceed to autologous transplant after complete metabolic response or a Deauville-4 partial metabolic response. 2 PARMA established transplant for chemosensitive relapse in the pre-rituximab era. Transplant improved 5-year EFS (46% vs 12%) and OS (53% vs 32%). Chemosensitivity defined the eligible population: 5-year OS was 42% among randomised responders but 11% among patients who never responded to DHAP. Salvage regimen choice can prioritise setting and toxicity because no regimen has established superior survival: CORAL found similar response and survival with R-ICE and R-DHAP. Three-year EFS was poor after prior rituximab and in refractory or early-relapsing disease; R-DHAP caused more platelet transfusions and grade 4 renal toxicity. NCIC-CTG LY.12 established noninferiority of GDP to DHAP for response after two cycles (140/310 vs 136/309 in ITT; noninferiority p=0.005). The subsequent gated test for a superior transplantation rate was not met (52.1% vs 49.3%; p=0.44). GDP caused less grade 3–4 toxicity, febrile neutropenia, transfusion and hospitalisation. HOVON 44 found better response and failure-free survival when rituximab was added to DHAP-VIM-DHAP, but no significant OS improvement. Only 4% had previously received rituximab, limiting current applicability. CAR T-cell therapy for patients not intended for transplant ALYCANTE enrolled and leukapheresed 69 transplant-ineligible patients after early treatment failure; 62 were infused. Among the infused patients, investigator-assessed 3-month CMR was 71% (44/62) and central-review CMR was 66% (41/62); median PFS from infusion was 11.8 months. Non-relapse mortality was 10% (6/62), entirely from infections occurring more than 2 months after infusion. PILOT evaluated lisocabtagene maraleucel after one prior line in patients not intended for transplant. Among 61 infused patients, ORR was 80% and CR 54%. Grade 3 or higher cytopenias persisted at day 28 in 30%; 12 of 74 leukapheresed patients were never infused. Third-line CAR T-cell therapy ZUMA-1 reported investigator-assessed ORR 82% and CR 54% with axicabtagene ciloleucel; independent review gave ORR 71%. CRS occurred in 93% and neurological events in 64%, with grade 3 or higher rates of 13% and 28%. Of 111 enrolled patients, 101 were infused. JULIET reported ORR 52% and CR 40% with tisagenlecleucel among evaluable patients. Only 111 of 165 enrolled patients were infused, at a median 54 days; 16 died before infusion. Responses were durable among those who achieved them. TRANSCEND NHL 001 reported ORR 73% and CR 53% with lisocabtagene maraleucel among infused evaluable patients. Fifteen percent of leukapheresed patients were not infused. Grade 3 or higher CRS occurred in 2% and neurological events in 10%, using a different CRS scale from JULIET.

records.title: Choose later-line antibody therapy by prior exposure and deliverability
records.subtitle: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma · Lymphoma
records.body: Bispecific antibodies and combinations STARGLO established glofitamab-GemOx over R-GemOx in transplant-ineligible relapsed/refractory DLBCL. Median OS was 25.5 versus 12.9 months (HR 0.62), median PFS 13.8 versus 3.6 months (HR 0.40), and CR 59% versus 25%. Glofitamab is fixed-duration for 12 cycles; grade 3 or higher adverse events occurred in 78% versus 41%. SUNMO established fixed-duration subcutaneous mosunetuzumab-polatuzumab over R-GemOx. ORR was 70% versus 40% and median PFS 11.5 versus 3.8 months (HR 0.41). Interim OS was not significant (HR 0.80, 95% CI 0.5–1.2). CRS occurred in 26%, with grade 3 events in 0.7%. For bispecific monotherapy after at least two prior lines: Glofitamab pivotal (NP30179) produced ORR 52% and CR 39% by independent review. Glofitamab stops after 12 cycles. CRS occurred in 63%, but grade 3 or higher events in 4%; one third had prior CAR T-cell therapy. EPCORE NHL-1 produced ORR 63% and CR 39% with subcutaneous epcoritamab given until progression. After prior CAR T-cell therapy, ORR was 54% and CR 34%. CRS occurred in 50%, largely after the first full dose; grade 3 CRS occurred in 2.5%. ELM-2 produced ORR 52% and CR 32% with odronextamab, but excluded previous CAR T-cell therapy. Grade 3 or higher infection occurred in 39%, and 15 patients died of infection. Antibody-drug and immunomodulatory combinations POLARGO improved OS with pola-R-GemOx over R-GemOx in patients ineligible for transplant and CAR T-cell therapy (median 19.5 vs 12.5 months; HR 0.60). Median PFS was 7.4 versus 2.7 months. Peripheral neuropathy and fatal adverse events were more frequent, although investigator-attributed treatment-related fatal events were similar. GO29365 compared pola-bendamustine-rituximab with bendamustine-rituximab in 80 patients. CR was 40% versus 18%, median PFS 9.5 versus 3.7 months and median OS 12.4 versus 4.7 months. The study was not powered to prove superiority, and haematological toxicity and neuropathy increased. L-MIND reported ORR 60%, CR 43% and median PFS 12.1 months with tafasitamab-lenalidomide in a single-arm, transplant-ineligible population. Primary refractory disease, known double-hit or triple-hit disease, CNS involvement and previous anti-CD19 therapy were excluded. RE-MIND2 matched the L-MIND cohort to real-world therapies. Conventional treatment produced median OS of approximately 10–12 months; comparisons favoured tafasitamab-lenalidomide but were non-randomised, used different response-assessment methods and were sponsor-conducted. LOTIS-2 reported ORR 48% and CR 24% with outpatient loncastuximab tesirine after at least two prior regimens. Median duration of response was 10.3 months. Oedema or effusion, skin or nail toxicity, gamma-glutamyl transferase elevation and cytopenias require monitoring. ECHELON-3 improved interim OS by adding brentuximab vedotin to lenalidomide-rituximab after at least two prior lines (median 13.8 vs 8.5 months; HR 0.63). Grade 3 or higher adverse events occurred in 88% versus 77%, including more neutropenia and thrombocytopenia.

records.title: Follow-up after complete metabolic response
records.subtitle: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma · Lymphoma
records.body: Routine surveillance PET-CT or diagnostic CT is generally not recommended after first-line treatment to complete metabolic response. Perform history and examination every 3–6 months for 2 years; follow-up may be discontinued after 2–5 years in asymptomatic patients. 2

records.title: Confirm the diagnosis and define the clinical group
records.subtitle: Hodgkin lymphoma · Lymphoma
records.body: Hodgkin lymphoma comprises classical Hodgkin lymphoma and nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma. Classical disease usually expresses CD15 and CD30 on Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg cells and lacks CD45. These malignant cells are derived from clonal B cells but have lost much of the normal B-cell phenotype. Classical Hodgkin lymphoma often presents with painless cervical, supraclavicular, axillary, inguinal or mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Spread is commonly contiguous. B symptoms are fever, drenching night sweats and significant unintentional weight loss. Nodular lymphocyte-predominant disease is usually more indolent but can transform to large B-cell lymphoma. Obtain adequate tissue, preferably by excisional or incisional lymph-node biopsy where feasible. Initial assessment includes a complete history and examination, full blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, renal and liver function, electrolytes and HIV testing. Assess cardiac function before doxorubicin and pulmonary function before bleomycin-containing treatment. Address fertility preservation before therapy.

records.title: Stage with PET-CT and retain the trial-specific response threshold
records.subtitle: Hodgkin lymphoma · Lymphoma
records.body: PET-CT is the principal staging and response-assessment modality in FDG-avid Hodgkin lymphoma. Routine marrow biopsy is unnecessary after adequate PET-CT staging unless unexplained cytopenias or a discordant marrow process would alter management. Surveillance imaging is discouraged after remission; clinical follow-up should also address late cardiopulmonary effects and second malignancies. Lugano Classification (Cheson et al.) Ann Arbor stage retains A or B symptom suffixes for Hodgkin lymphoma. Contiguous extranodal extension may be labelled E; disseminated extranodal disease is stage IV. Bulky disease includes a nodal mass greater than 10 cm or a mediastinal mass wider than one-third of the transthoracic diameter. Treatment planning separates early favourable, early unfavourable and advanced disease. The GHSG early-unfavourable factors are a large mediastinal mass, extranodal involvement, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and at least 3 involved nodal areas. Elevated ESR means at least 50 mm/hour without B symptoms or at least 30 mm/hour with them. Advanced-stage prognosis can be described with the International Prognostic Score. The stage-IIB boundary differs across the GHSG programmes. HD14 and HD17 admitted stage IIB only when raised ESR or at least 3 involved nodal areas was present and bulky mediastinal or extranodal disease was absent. HD18 and HD21 instead classified stage IIB with B symptoms plus a bulky mediastinal mass and/or extranodal disease as advanced-stage disease. Deauville score 3 is handled differently across response-adapted trials. HD16, HD17, UK RAPID, H10 and HD18 assigned score 3 to the positive group. RATHL assigned scores 1-3 to the negative group. Apply the cut-point from the regimen and trial being followed rather than a universal definition.

records.title: Early favourable disease: reduce treatment only within tested boundaries
records.subtitle: Hodgkin lymphoma · Lymphoma
records.body: Two cycles of ABVD followed by 20 Gy involved-field radiotherapy is the least intensive combined-modality regimen established in the GHSG favourable population. Omitting radiotherapy after a negative interim PET reduces tumour control. A chemotherapy-only choice therefore accepts more relapse to avoid radiotherapy exposure; the cited trials did not show a survival difference at their reported follow-up. GHSG HD7 established the value of adding chemotherapy to radiotherapy. Among 650 patients with favourable early-stage disease, 7-year freedom from treatment failure was 88% with 2 cycles of ABVD before extended-field radiotherapy and 67% with radiotherapy alone. Seven-year overall survival was 94% and 92%, respectively. GHSG HD10 randomised 1,370 patients in a 2 by 2 factorial comparison of 4 versus 2 ABVD cycles and 30 versus 20 Gy radiotherapy. Five-year freedom from treatment failure was 91.1% versus 93.0% for 2 versus 4 cycles and 92.9% versus 93.4% for 20 versus 30 Gy. Both reductions met the 7-point non-inferiority margin and caused less acute toxicity. GHSG HD13 tested whether ABVD itself could be reduced; all arms received 30 Gy involved-field radiotherapy. The dacarbazine-omitted ABV and AV arms closed early for higher event rates and could be compared with concurrent ABVD only descriptively. AVD completed accrual but did not establish non-inferiority to ABVD (5-year freedom from treatment failure 89.2% versus 93.1%; hazard ratio 1.50, 95% CI 1.00-2.26). Neither dacarbazine nor bleomycin should be omitted from this 2-cycle combined-modality programme. GHSG HD16 randomised 1,150 patients before interim PET. Among 628 PET-2-negative patients analysed per protocol, omitting 20 Gy radiotherapy after 2 ABVD cycles reduced 5-year progression-free survival from 93.4% to 86.1% (difference -7.3 points, 95% CI -13.0 to -1.6). In-field recurrence was 9% without radiotherapy and 2% with it; 5-year overall survival was 98.4% without radiotherapy versus 98.1% with it, an underpowered secondary comparison that did not demonstrate a survival difference. ABVD is administered on days 1 and 15 of a 28-day cycle: doxorubicin 25 mg/m², bleomycin 10 units/m², vinblastine 6 mg/m² and dacarbazine 375 mg/m². Confirm the exact product expression, administration and supportive-care protocol before prescribing.

records.title: Early unfavourable disease: choose between combined modality and intensified PET adaptation
records.subtitle: Hodgkin lymphoma · Lymphoma
records.body: Four cycles of ABVD followed by 30 Gy involved-field radiotherapy is the comparator established in the GHSG early-unfavourable programme. The intensified 2+2 approach, 2 cycles of escalated BEACOPP followed by 2 cycles of ABVD, improves tumour control but increases acute haematological toxicity. PET-guided radiotherapy omission is established only after that intensified backbone. GHSG HD8 reduced the radiotherapy field. In 1,204 patients with early unfavourable disease or stage IIIA without risk factors, involved-field radiotherapy preserved 5-year freedom from treatment failure compared with extended-field treatment (84.2% versus 85.8%) and reduced acute nausea, leucopenia and thrombocytopenia. GHSG HD11 compared ABVD with baseline BEACOPP and 30 with 20 Gy radiotherapy. After ABVD, 20 Gy did not establish non-inferiority to 30 Gy (5-year freedom-from-treatment-failure difference -4.7 points, 95% CI -10.3 to 0.8). Baseline BEACOPP was more toxic and did not improve on ABVD when both were followed by 30 Gy. GHSG HD14 compared 2 cycles of escalated BEACOPP plus 2 cycles of ABVD with 4 cycles of ABVD, both followed by 30 Gy. Five-year freedom from treatment failure was 94.8% versus 87.7% (hazard ratio 0.44, 95% CI 0.30-0.66), without a shown survival gain. Grade 4 toxicity occurred in 56.6% versus 5.9%. GHSG HD17 tested radiotherapy omission after the intensified 2+2 backbone. In the per-protocol population, 5-year progression-free survival was 95.1% with PET-guided treatment and 97.3% with radiotherapy for all. The upper confidence bound of 5.3 points remained inside the 8-point non-inferiority margin. PET negativity was Deauville 1-2. UK RAPID enrolled 602 patients and tested omission after 3 ABVD cycles. Among 420 PET-negative patients, 3-year progression-free survival was 90.8% without radiotherapy and 94.6% with it. The confidence interval for the -3.8-point difference extended to -8.8 points, outside the 7-point margin. PET negativity was Deauville 1-2. EORTC/LYSA/FIL H10 enrolled 1,950 patients and failed to establish radiotherapy omission after negative PET-2. Five-year progression-free survival was 87.1% without radiotherapy versus 99.0% with it in favourable disease and 89.6% versus 92.1% in unfavourable disease. In PET-positive patients, escalation improved 5-year progression-free survival from 77.4% to 90.6% (hazard ratio 0.42, 95% CI 0.23-0.74) but increased acute toxicity. In the PET-positive comparison, 5-year overall survival was 89.3% with continued ABVD versus 96.0% with escalation (hazard ratio 0.45; P=0.062), a difference that was not statistically significant. H10 defined Deauville 1-2 as negative and 3-5 as positive.

records.title: Advanced disease: match efficacy gains to toxicity and maturity
records.subtitle: Hodgkin lymphoma · Lymphoma
records.body: Phase III trials support several frontline approaches in advanced classical Hodgkin lymphoma. Their populations are not interchangeable: ECHELON-1 enrolled stage III-IV adults, S1826 enrolled patients aged 12 years or older with stage III-IV disease, and HD21 enrolled patients aged 18-60 years within the GHSG advanced-stage definition. In HD21, PET-2-guided treatment length was introduced by amendment and applied to 1,346 of 1,482 analysed patients (91%), not uniformly to the entire randomised comparison. Historical escalated-BEACOPP programme GHSG HD9 compared escalated BEACOPP with baseline BEACOPP and the older COPP/ABVD regimen, not ABVD alone. At 10 years, freedom from treatment failure was 82%, 70% and 64%, and overall survival 86%, 80% and 75%. Secondary leukaemia or myelodysplasia increased with dose; the 10-year comparisons were outside the prespecified analysis schedule. GHSG HD15 established that 6 cycles of escalated BEACOPP were non-inferior to 8 and less toxic. Five-year freedom from treatment failure was 89.3% with 6 cycles and 84.4% with 8. Treatment-related death was 0.8% versus 2.1%, and secondary leukaemia or myelodysplasia 0.3% versus 2.7%. GHSG HD18 used PET after 2 escalated-BEACOPP cycles to answer 2 questions. Rituximab did not improve 5-year progression-free survival in PET-positive disease (88.1% versus 89.7%; hazard ratio 1.25, 95% CI 0.69-2.26). In PET-negative disease, 4 total cycles were non-inferior to 6-8 and caused fewer severe infections and treatment-related deaths. Deauville 3 counted as positive. Brentuximab, nivolumab and BrECADD ECHELON-1 compared brentuximab vedotin plus AVD with ABVD in 1,334 patients. Modified progression-free survival at 2 years was 82.1% versus 77.2% (hazard ratio 0.77, 95% CI 0.60-0.98). Interstitial lung disease fell from 7% to 2%, while neuropathy rose from 43% to 67% and febrile neutropenia from 8% to 19%. At median follow-up 72.6 months, investigator-assessed 6-year progression-free survival was 82.3% versus 74.5% (hazard ratio 0.68; 95% CI 0.53-0.86); this analysis was outside the testing hierarchy and descriptive. The alpha-protected second interim overall-survival analysis at median follow-up 73 months favoured brentuximab vedotin plus AVD (6-year overall survival 93.9% versus 89.4%; hazard ratio 0.59, 95% CI 0.40-0.88; P=0.009). Primary G-CSF prophylaxis was recommended after enrolment had begun; the initial efficacy result was not generated under uniform prophylaxis. SWOG S1826 compared nivolumab plus AVD with brentuximab vedotin plus AVD in 994 patients. The planned interim analysis showed a progression-free-survival advantage (hazard ratio 0.48, 99% CI 0.27-0.87; 1-year rate 94% versus 86%). A later cut gave 2-year rates of 92% versus 83%. Whole-trial overall survival remains immature and unproven (hazard ratio 0.39, 95% CI 0.15-1.03). Both age reports were planned but unprotected subset analyses and neither reported an age-by-treatment interaction test. The older analysis used age at least 60 years, which differs from the parent trial's older-than-60 randomisation stratum. At median follow-up 25.2 months, it reported 3 deaths among 50 patients with nivolumab plus AVD and 10 among 49 with brentuximab vedotin plus AVD. At median follow-up 37.2 months, the adolescent analysis reported 3-year progression-free survival of 93% versus 82%. Grade 3 or worse neutropenia was more frequent with nivolumab, but G-CSF was mandatory only in the brentuximab arm. GHSG HD21 randomised 1,500 patients and analysed 1,482. Treatment-related-morbidity superiority was tested first and met: 42% with BrECADD versus 59% with escalated BEACOPP (relative risk 0.72, 95% CI 0.65-0.80). Gated progression-free-survival non-inferiority then met. After the successful interim analysis, a protocol amendment added a final superiority test using the remaining two-sided alpha; 4-year progression-free survival was 94.3% versus 90.9% (hazard ratio 0.66, 95% CI 0.45-0.97), and P=0.035 crossed the prespecified 0.0392 boundary. Consolidative radiotherapy for PET-positive residual disease in HD21 was not randomised and was received by 15% with BrECADD and 14% with escalated BEACOPP. BrECADD reduced grade 3 or worse anaemia and thrombocytopenia and improved gonadal recovery, but did not reduce every toxicity. Organ toxicity was 19% versus 17%, and neutropenic fever, cardiac and gastrointestinal events were more frequent with BrECADD. Four-year overall survival was 98.6% versus 98.2%. ABVD with PET-guided bleomycin omission RATHL enrolled adults with stage IIB-IV disease or stage IIA disease with bulky disease or at least 3 involved sites. It randomised 935 patients who were PET-negative after 2 ABVD cycles, defined as Deauville 1-3, to continue ABVD or omit bleomycin for cycles 3-6. Three-year progression-free survival was 85.7% versus 84.4%. The confidence interval for the 1.6-point difference extended to 5.3 points, just beyond the 5-point non-inferiority margin, while pulmonary toxicity was lower with AVD. The 172 PET-positive patients escalated to BEACOPP without a randomised ABVD comparator and had 3-year progression-free survival of 67.5%. This cohort supports feasibility of escalation but cannot establish its benefit over continuing ABVD.

records.title: Relapsed or refractory disease: separate transplant intent from later-line control
records.subtitle: Hodgkin lymphoma · Lymphoma
records.body: Confirm relapse histologically where feasible and restage before treatment. Of 166 patients assessed in HD-R1, 5 were excluded before randomisation and 161 were randomised upfront before shared Dexa-BEAM induction. Among 144 assessable patients, 117 achieved complete or partial response after 2 cycles and proceeded to their assigned further Dexa-BEAM or high-dose BEAM plus autologous-transplant arm; the primary per-protocol result applies to those 117. GHSG/EBMT HD-R1 established autologous transplantation in chemosensitive relapse. In the 117-patient per-protocol set, 3-year freedom from treatment failure was 55% after high-dose BEAM and transplant versus 34% with further Dexa-BEAM (P=0.019); nominal overall survival was 71% versus 65% without a demonstrated difference. Brentuximab vedotin (pivotal) evaluated 102 patients after autologous transplant had failed. Independent-review objective response was 75% (95% CI 64.9-82.6), including 34% complete response. Median progression-free survival was 5.6 months overall and 21.7 months among complete responders. Peripheral sensory neuropathy occurred in 42%, including 8% grade 3. AETHERA randomised 329 high-risk patients after autologous transplant to brentuximab vedotin or placebo. Median independent-review progression-free survival was 42.9 versus 24.1 months (hazard ratio 0.57, 95% CI 0.40-0.81). Overall survival did not differ at the interim analysis, with substantial post-progression crossover to brentuximab in the placebo group. CheckMate 205 evaluated nivolumab in 80 patients whose disease progressed after autologous transplant and subsequent brentuximab vedotin. Independent-review objective response was 66.3% (95% CI 54.8-76.4), including 9% complete response. Median response duration was 7.8 months and median progression-free survival 10.0 months at a median follow-up of 8.9 months. KEYNOTE-204 compared pembrolizumab with brentuximab vedotin in 304 patients after autologous transplant or judged transplant-ineligible. Median progression-free survival was 13.2 versus 8.3 months (hazard ratio 0.65, 95% CI 0.48-0.88). Overall survival, a co-primary endpoint, had not been analysed at the reported interim cut.
